author: Gotama Buddha
text: When anger surges, they drive it out, as with medicine a cobra's spreading venom. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've cut off greed entirely, like a lotus plucked flower and stalk. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've cut off craving entirely, drying up that swift-flowing stream. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've swept away conceit entirely, as a fragile bridge of reeds by a great flood. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: In future lives they find no worth, as an inspector of fig trees finds no flower. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They hide no anger within, passed beyond any kind of existence. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Their mental vibrations are cleared away, internally clipped off entirely. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have not run too far nor run back, but have gone beyond all this proliferation. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have not run too far nor run back, for they know that nothing in the world is what it seems. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have not run too far nor run back, knowing nothing is what it seems, free of greed. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have not run too far nor run back, knowing nothing is what it seems, free of lust. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have not run too far nor run back, knowing nothing is what it seems, free of hate. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have not run too far nor run back, knowing nothing is what it seems, free of delusion. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have no underlying tendencies at all, and are rid of unskillful roots, Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have nothing born of distress at all to make them to return to the near shore. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: No snarl grows in them at all, that would shackle them to a new life. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've given up the five hindrances, untroubled, rid of indecision, free of thorns. Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far, as a serpent its old worn-out skin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I've boiled my rice and drawn my milk," said Dhaniya the rancher, "I stay with my family along the bank of the Mahī. My hut is roofed, my sacred fire kindled: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I boil not with anger and have drawn out hard-heartedness," said the Buddha, "I stay for one night along the bank of the Mahī. My hut is wide open, my fire is quenched: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "No gadflies or mosquitoes are found," said Dhaniya, "cows graze on the lush meadow grass. They get by even when the rain comes: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I bound a raft and prepared it well," said the Buddha, "and with it I crossed over, went to the far shore, and dispelled the flood. Now I have no need for a raft: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "My wife is obedient, not wanton," said Dhaniya, "long have we lived together happily. I hear nothing bad about her: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "My mind is obedient and freed," said the Buddha, "long nurtured and well-tamed. Nothing bad is found in me: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I am self-employed," said Dhaniya, "and my healthy children likewise. I hear nothing bad about them: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I am no one's lackey," said the Buddha, "with what I have earned I wander the world. I have no need for wages: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I have heifers and sucklings," said Dhaniya, "cows in calf and breeding cows. I've also got a bull, captain of the herd here: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I have no heifers or sucklings," said the Buddha, "no cows in calf or breeding cows. I haven't got a bull, captain of the herd here: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The stakes are driven in, unshakable," said Dhaniya, "The grass halters are new and well-woven, not even the sucklings can break them: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Like a bull I broke the bonds," said the Buddha, "like an elephant I snapped the vine. I will never lie in a womb again: so rain forth, heavens, if you wish."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Right then a vast cloud rained forth, soaking the uplands and valleys. Hearing the heavens rain down, Dhaniya said this:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "It is no small gain for us that we have seen the Buddha. We come to you for refuge, Clear-eyed One. O great sage, please be our Teacher.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: My wife and I, obedient, shall lead the spiritual life under the Holy One. Gone beyond birth and death, we shall make an end of suffering."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Children bring you delight!" said Māra the Wicked, "Cattle also bring you delight! For attachments are a man's delight; without attachments there's no delight."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Your children bring you sorrow," said the Buddha, "Your cattle also bring you sorrow. For attachments are a man's sorrow; without attachments there are no sorrows."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When you've laid down violence toward all creatures, not harming even a single one, don't wish for a child, let alone a companion: live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those with close relationships have affection, following which this pain arises. Seeing this danger born of affection, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When feelings for friends and loved ones are tied up in selfish love, you miss out on the goal. Seeing this peril in intimacy, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As a spreading bamboo gets entangled, so does concern for partners and children. Like a bamboo shoot unobstructed, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As a wild deer loose in the forest grazes wherever it wants, a smart person looking for freedom would live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When among friends, whether staying in place or going on a journey, you're always on call. Looking for the uncoveted freedom, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Among friends you have fun and games, and for children you are full of fondness. Though loathe to depart from those you hold dear, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: At ease in any quarter, unresisting, content with whatever comes your way; prevailing over adversities, dauntless, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Even some renunciates are hard to please, as are some layfolk dwelling at home. Don't worry about others' children, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having shed the marks of the home life, like the fallen leaves of the Shady Orchid Tree; having cut the bonds of the home life, a hero would live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If you find an alert companion, an attentive friend to live happily together, then, overcoming all adversities, wander with them, joyful and mindful.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If you find no alert companion, an attentive friend to live happily together, then, like a king who flees his conquered realm, wander alone like a tusker in the wilds.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Clearly we praise the blessing of a friend, it's good to be with friends your equal or better. But failing to find them, eating blamelessly, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Though made of shining gold, well-finished by a smith, when two bracelets share the same arm they clash up against each other. Seeing this, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Thinking, "So too, if I had a partner, there'd be flattery or curses." Seeing this peril in the future, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Sensual pleasures are diverse, sweet, delightful; appearing in disguise they disturb the mind. Seeing danger in sensual stimulations, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: This is a calamity, a boil, a disaster, an illness, a dart, and a danger for me. Seeing this peril in sensuality, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Heat and cold, hunger and thirst, wind and sun, flies and reptiles: having put up with all these things, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As a full-grown elephant, lotus-fond, magnificent, forsaking the herd, stays as it pleases in the forest, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: It's impossible for one who delights in company to experience even temporary freedom. Heeding the speech of the Kinsman of the Sun, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Thinking, "I have left twisted views behind, reached the sure way, and gained the path; I've given rise to knowledge, and need no one to guide me", live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: No greed, no guile, no thirst, no slur, dross and delusion is smelted off; free of hoping for anything in the world, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Avoid a wicked companion, blind to the good, habitually immoral. Don't befriend the heedless and the hankering, but live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Spend time with the learned who have memorized the teachings, an eloquent and uplifting friend. When you understand the meanings and have dispelled doubt, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When you realize that worldly fun and games and pleasure are inadequate, unconcerned with them, as one unadorned, a speaker of truth, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Children, partner, father, mother, wealth and grain and relatives: having given up sensual pleasures to this extent, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "This is a chain. Here there's hardly any happiness, little gratification, and it's full of drawbacks. It's a hook." Knowing this, a thoughtful person would live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having burst apart the fetters, like a fish that tears the net and swims free, or a fire not returning to ground it has burned, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Eyes downcast, not footloose, senses guarded, mind protected, not festering or burning with desire, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having shed the marks of the home life, like the fallen leaves of the Orchid Tree, and gone forth in the ocher robe, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not wanton, nor rousing greed for tastes, providing for no other, wandering indiscriminately for alms, not attached to this family or that, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When you've given up five mental obstacles, and cast aside all corruptions, and cut off affection and hate, being independent, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When you've put pleasure and pain behind you, and former happiness and sadness, and gained equanimity serene and pure, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: With energy roused to reach the ultimate goal, not sluggish in mind or lazy, vigorous, strong and powerful, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not neglecting retreat and absorption, always living in line with the teaching, comprehending the danger in rebirths, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One whose aim is the ending of craving— diligent, clever, learned, mindful, resolute— who has appraised the teaching and is assured, destined for awakening, should live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Like a lion not startled by sounds, like wind not caught in a net, like water not sticking to a lotus, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Like the fierce-fanged lion, king of beasts, who wanders as conqueror and victor, you should frequent remote lodgings, and live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: In time, cultivate freedom through love, compassion, rejoicing, and equanimity. Not upset by anything in the world, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having given up greed, hate, and delusion, having burst apart the fetters, unafraid at the end of life, live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They befriend you and serve you for their own sake; these days it's hard to find friends lacking ulterior motive. Impure folk cleverly profit themselves— live alone like a horned rhino.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Magadhans in the Southern Hills near the brahmin village of Ekanāḷa. Now at that time the brahmin Bhāradvāja the Farmer had harnessed around five hundred plows, it being the season for sowing. Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to where Bhāradvāja the Farmer was working. Now at that time Bhāradvāja the Farmer was distributing food. Then the Buddha went to where the distribution was taking place and stood to one side.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Bhāradvāja the Farmer saw him standing for alms and said to him, "I plough and sow, ascetic, and then I eat. You too should plough and sow, then you may eat."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I too plough and sow, brahmin, and then I eat." "I don't see the worthy Gotama with a yoke or plow or plowshare or goad or oxen, yet he says: 'I too plough and sow, brahmin, and then I eat.'"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Bhāradvāja the Farmer addressed the Buddha in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "You claim to be a farmer, but I don't see you farming. Tell me your farming when asked, so I can recognize your farming."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Faith is my seed, fervor my rain, and wisdom is my yoke and plough. Conscience is my draft-pole, mind my strap, mindfulness my plowshare and goad.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Guarded in body and speech, I restrict my intake of food. I use truth as my scythe, and gentleness is my release.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Energy is my harnessed beast, transporting me to sanctuary from the yoke. Without turning back, it goes to where there is no sorrow.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That's how to do the farming that has freedom from death as its fruit. When you finish this farming you're released from all suffering."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Bhāradvāja the Farmer poured milk-rice in a large bronze cup and presented it to the Buddha: "May the worthy Gotama eat the milk-rice! The worthy one is a farmer. For the worthy Gotama does the farming that has freedom from death as its fruit."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Food enchanted by a verse isn't fit for me to eat. That's not the principle of those who see, brahmin. The Buddhas cast aside things enchanted with verses. Since there is such a principle, brahmin, that's how they live.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Serve with other food and drink the consummate one, the great seer, with defilements ended and remorse stilled. For he is the field for the seeker of merit."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Then, worthy Gotama, to whom should I give the milk-rice?" "Brahmin, I don't see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who can properly digest this milk-rice, except the Realized One or one of his disciples. Well then, brahmin, throw out the milk-rice where there is little that grows, or drop it into water that has no living creatures."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So Bhāradvāja the Farmer dropped the milk-rice in water that had no living creatures. And when the milk-rice was placed in the water, it sizzled and hissed, steaming and fuming. Suppose there was an iron cauldron that had been heated all day. If you placed it in the water, it would sizzle and hiss, steaming and fuming. In the same way, when the milk-rice was placed in the water, it sizzled and hissed, steaming and fuming.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Bhāradvāja the Farmer, shocked and awestruck, went up to the Buddha, bowed down with his head to the Buddha's feet, and said, "Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what's there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways. I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha. May I receive the going forth, the ordination in the worthy Gotama's presence?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And Bhāradvāja the Farmer received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha's presence. Not long after his ordination, Venerable Bhāradvāja, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness. He understood: "Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place." And Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the perfected.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I ask the sage abounding in wisdom," said Cunda the smith, "the Buddha, master of the teaching, free of craving, best of men, excellent charioteer, please tell me this: how many ascetics are there in the world?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "There are four ascetics, not a fifth." said the Buddha to Cunda, "Being asked to bear witness, I will explain them to you: the path-victor, the path-teacher, the path-liver, and the path-wrecker."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Who is a path-victor according to the Buddhas?" said Cunda the smith, "and how is one an unequaled explainer of the path? Tell me when asked about one who lives the path, then declare the path-wrecker."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Rid of indecision, free of thorns, delighting in extinguishment, not fawning, a guide for the world with its gods. The Buddhas say one such is victor of the path.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing the ultimate as ultimate, they explain and analyze the teaching right here. That sage unstirred, with doubt cut off, is the second mendicant, I say, the teacher of the path.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Living restrained and mindful on the path of the well-taught passage of teaching, cultivating blameless states, is the third mendicant, I say, the path-liver.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Dressed like one true to their vows, pushy, rude, a corrupter of families, devious, unrestrained, chaff, the path-wrecker's life is a sham.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A layperson who gets this, a learned, wise noble disciple, knows that 'They are not all like that one'. So when they see them they don't lose their faith. For how could one equate them— the corrupt with the uncorrupt, the pure with the impure?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta's Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity addressed the Buddha in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We ask Gotama about a man's downfall. We have come to ask you, sir: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "It's easy to understand success, understanding downfall is just as easy. One who loves the teaching succeeds, but a hater of the teaching meets their downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the first downfall. Tell us the second, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The bad are dear to him, he has no love for the good. He believes the teaching of the bad; and that leads to his downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the second downfall. Tell us the third, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Fond of sleep, fond of company, a man who does no work; he's lazy, marked by anger, and that leads to his downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the third downfall. Tell us the fourth, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Though able, he does not look after his mother and father when elderly, past their prime, and that leads to his downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the fourth downfall. Tell us the fifth, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "He deceives with lies ascetics and brahmins and other supplicants, and that leads to his downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the fifth downfall. Tell us the sixth, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "A man with plenty of wealth, including gold coin and food, eats delicacies alone, and that leads to his downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the sixth downfall. Tell us the seventh, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Vain of birth, wealth, and clan, a man looks down on his own family, and that leads to his downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the seventh downfall. Tell us the eighth, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "In womanizing, drinking, and gambling, a man wastes all that he has earned, and that leads to his downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the eighth downfall. Tell us the ninth, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Not content with his own partners, he debauches himself with prostitutes, and with others' partners, and that leads to his downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the ninth downfall. Tell us the tenth, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "A man well past his prime marries a girl with budding breasts; he cannot sleep for jealousy, and that leads to his downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the tenth downfall. Tell us the eleventh, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "He places in authority a woman or a man who's a drunkard and a wastrel, and that leads to his downfall."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We understand what you're saying, this is the eleventh downfall. Tell us the twelfth, Blessed One: what leads to downfall?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "A man of little wealth and strong craving, born into an aristocratic family, sets his sights on kingship, and that leads to his downfall.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Seeing these downfalls in the world, an astute and noble person, accomplished in vision, will enjoy a world of grace."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Now at that time in the brahmin Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper's home the sacred flame had been kindled and the oblation prepared. Wandering indiscriminately for almsfood in Sāvatthī, the Buddha approached Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper's house.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper saw the Buddha coming off in the distance and said to him, "Stop right there, shaveling! Right there, fake ascetic! Right there, lowlife!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When he said this, the Buddha said to him, "But brahmin, do you know what is a lowlife or what are the qualities that make you a lowlife?" "No I do not, worthy Gotama. Please, worthy Gotama, teach me this matter so I can understand what is a lowlife or what are the qualities that make you a lowlife." "Well then, brahmin, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak." "Yes, worthy sir," Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper replied. The Buddha said this:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Irritable and acrimonious, wicked and offensive, a man deficient in view, deceitful: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He harms living creatures born of womb or of egg, and has no kindness for creatures: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He destroys and devastates villages and towns, a notorious oppressor: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Whether in village or wilderness, he steals what belongs to others, taking what has not been given: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having fallen into debt, when pressed to pay up he flees, saying 'I don't owe you anything!': know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Wanting some item or other, he attacks a person in the street and takes it: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For his own sake or the sake of another, or for the sake of wealth, a man tells a lie when asked to bear witness: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He is spied among the partners of relatives and friends, by force or seduction: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Though able, he does not look after his mother and father when elderly, past their prime: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He hits or verbally abuses his mother or father, brother, sister, or mother-in-law: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When asked about the good, he teaches what is bad, giving secretive advice: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having done a bad deed, he wishes, 'May no one find me out!' His deeds are underhand: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When visiting another family he eats their delicious food, but does not return the honor: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He deceives with lies ascetics and brahmins and other supplicants: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When time comes to offer a meal to brahmins or ascetics, he abuses them and does not give: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He talks about what never happened, being wrapped up in delusion, chasing after some item or other: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He extols himself and disparages others, brought down by his pride: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He's a bully and a miser, of corrupt wishes, stingy, and devious, shameless, imprudent: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He insults the Buddha or his disciple, whether lay or renunciate: know him as a lowlife.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He claims to be a perfected one, when he really is no such thing. In the world with its divinities, that crook is truly the lowest lowlife. These who are called lowlifes I have revealed to you.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You're not a lowlife by birth, nor by birth are you a brahmin. You're a lowlife by your deeds, by deeds you're a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And also you should know according to this example. A corpse-worker's son of the dog-eating caste became renowned as Mātaṅga.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Mātaṅga achieved the highest fame so very hard to find. Lots of aristocrats and brahmins came to serve him.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He ascended the stainless highway that leads to the heavens; having discarded sensual desire, he was reborn in a realm of divinity. His birth did not prevent him from rebirth in the realm of divinity.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those born in a brahmin family who recite as kinsmen of the hymns, are often discovered in the midst of wicked deeds.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Blameworthy in this very life, and in lives to come, a bad destination. Their birth does not prevent them from blame or bad destiny.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You're not a lowlife by birth, nor by birth are you a brahmin. You're a lowlife by your deeds, by deeds you're a brahmin."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When he had spoken, the brahmin Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper said to the Buddha, "Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! … From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those who are skilled in the meaning of scripture should practice as follows to realize the state of peace. Let them be capable and upright, very upright, easy to speak to, gentle and humble;

author: Gotama Buddha
text: content and unburdensome, unbusied, living lightly, alert, with senses calmed, courteous, not fawning on families.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Let them not do the slightest thing that others who are wise would blame. May they be happy and safe! May all beings be happy!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Whatever living creatures there are with not a one left out— frail or firm, long or large, medium, small, tiny or round,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: seen or unseen, living far or near, those who have been born and those about to be born— may all beings be happy!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Let none deceive another, nor look down on anyone anywhere. Though provoked or aggrieved, let them not wish pain on each other.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Even as a mother would protect with her life her child, her only child, so too for all creatures unfold a boundless heart.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: With love for the whole world, unfold a boundless heart: above, below, all round, unconstricted, without enmity or foe.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When standing, walking, sitting, or lying down while yet unweary, keep this ever in mind; for this, they say, is a divine meditation in this life.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Avoiding harmful views, virtuous, accomplished in insight, with desire for sensual pleasures dispelled, they never return to a womb again.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Today is the fifteenth day sabbath," said Sātāgira, the native spirit of mount Sātā, "a holy night is at hand. Come now, let us see Gotama, the Teacher of peerless name."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Isn't his mind well-disposed," said Hemavata, the native spirit of the Himalayas, "impartial toward all creatures? And aren't his thoughts under control when it comes to likes and dislikes?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "His mind is well-disposed," said Sātāgira, "impartial toward all creatures. His thoughts are under control when it comes to his likes and dislikes."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Doesn't he not steal?" said Hemavata, "And doesn't he harm not a creature? Isn't he far from negligence? And doesn't he not neglect absorption?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "He does not take what is not given," said Sātāgira, "and he harms not a creature. He is far from negligence— the Buddha does not neglect absorption."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Doesn't he avoid lying?" said Hemavata, "And doesn't he not speak sharply? Doesn't he avoid backbiting, as well as speaking nonsense?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "He does not lie," said Sātāgira, "nor does he speak sharply. He avoids backbiting, and thoughtfully speaks wise counsel."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Doesn't he find sensual pleasures unattractive?" said Hemavata, "And isn't his mind unclouded? Hasn't he escaped delusion? Does his eye see clearly in all things?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "He does not find sensual pleasures attractive," said Sātāgira, "and his mind is unclouded. He has escaped all delusion— the Buddha, whose eye sees clearly in all things."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Isn't he accomplished in knowledge?" said Hemavata, "And doesn't he live a pure life? Aren't his defilements all ended? Doesn't he have no future lives?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "He is accomplished in knowledge," said Sātāgira, "and he does live a pure life. His defilements are all ended, there'll be no more future lives for him."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Accomplished is the sage's mind in action and in speech, and he's accomplished in knowledge and conduct as per the teaching you praise."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Accomplished is the sage's mind in action and in speech, and he's accomplished in knowledge and conduct as per the teaching you rejoice in.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Accomplished is the sage's mind in action and in speech, and he's accomplished in knowledge and conduct: come now, let us see Gotama."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The hero so lean, with antelope calves, not greedy, eating little, the sage meditating alone in the forest, come now, let us see Gotama.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A giant, wandering alone like a lion, unconcerned for sensual pleasures, let's approach him and ask about release from the snare of death."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The communicator, the instructor, who has gone beyond all things, Awakened, beyond enmities and fears, let us ask Gotama."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "What has the world arisen in?" said Hemavata, "What does it get close to? By grasping what is the world troubled in what?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The world's arisen in six," said the Buddha to Hemavata. "It gets close to six. Derived from the six, the world's troubled in six."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "What is that grasping by which the world is troubled? Tell us the exit when asked: how is one released from all suffering?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The world has five kinds of sensual stimulation, and the mind is said to be the sixth. When you've discarded desire for these, you're released from all suffering.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: This is the exit from the world, explained in accord with the truth. The way I've explained it is how you're released from all suffering."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Who here crosses the flood, Who crosses the deluge? Who, not standing and unsupported, does not sink in the deep?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Someone who is always endowed with ethics, wise and serene, inwardly reflective, mindful, crosses the flood so hard to cross.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Someone who desists from sensual perception, who has escaped all fetters, and has ended relish for rebirth, does not sink in the deep."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Behold him of wisdom deep who sees the subtle meaning, who has nothing, unattached to sensual life, everywhere free, the great seer treading the holy road.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Behold him of peerless name who sees the subtle meaning, giver of wisdom, unattached to the realm of sensuality: the all-knower, so very intelligent, the great seer treading the noble road.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: It was a fine sight for us today, a good sunup, a good rising, to see the Awakened One, the undefiled one who has crossed the flood.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: These thousand native spirits powerful and glorious, all go to you for refuge, you are our supreme Teacher.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: We shall journey village to village, peak to peak, paying homage to the Buddha, and the clear rightness of the teaching!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Āḷavī in the haunt of the native spirit Āḷavaka. Then the native spirit Āḷavaka went up to the Buddha, and said to him: "Get out, ascetic!" Saying, "All right, respectable sir," the Buddha went out. "Get in, ascetic!" Saying, "All right, respectable sir," the Buddha went in.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For a second time … And for a third time the native spirit Āḷavaka said to the Buddha, "Get out, ascetic!" Saying, "All right, respectable sir," the Buddha went out. "Get in, ascetic!" Saying, "All right, respectable sir," the Buddha went in.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And for a fourth time the native spirit Āḷavaka said to the Buddha, "Get out, ascetic!" "No, respectable sir, I won't get out. Do what you must."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I will ask you a question, ascetic. If you don't answer me, I'll drive you insane, or explode your heart, or grab you by the feet and throw you to the far shore of the Ganges!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I don't see anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans who could do that to me. But anyway, ask what you wish." Then the native spirit Āḷavaka addressed the Buddha in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "What's a person's best wealth? What brings happiness when practiced well? What's the sweetest taste of all? The one they say has the best life: how do they live?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Faith here is a person's best wealth. The teaching brings happiness when practiced well. Truth is the sweetest taste of all. The one they say has the best life lives by wisdom."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "How do you cross the flood? How do you cross the deluge? How do you get over suffering? How do you get purified?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "By faith you cross the flood, and by diligence the deluge. By energy you get past suffering, and you're purified by wisdom."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "How do you get wisdom? How do you earn wealth? How do you get a good reputation? How do you hold on to friends? How do the departed not grieve when passing from this world to the next?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "One who is diligent and discerning gains wisdom by wanting to learn, having faith in the perfected ones, and the teaching for becoming extinguished.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Being responsible, acting appropriately, and working hard you earn wealth. Truthfulness wins you a good reputation. You hold on to friends by giving.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A faithful householder of discernment who possesses these four qualities does not grieve after passing away: truth, principle, steadfastness, and generosity.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Go ahead, ask others as well, there are many ascetics and brahmins. See whether anything better is found than truth, principle, generosity, and patience."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Why now would I question the many ascetics and brahmins? Today I understand what's good for lives to come.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: It was truly for my benefit that the Buddha came to stay at Āḷavī. Today I understand where a gift is very fruitful.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: I myself will journey village to village, town to town, paying homage to the Buddha, and the clear rightness of the teaching!"

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: Walking and standing, sitting and lying down, extending and contracting the limbs: these are the movements of the body.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: Linked together by bones and sinews, plastered over with flesh and hide, and covered by the skin, the body is not seen as it is.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: It's full of guts and belly, liver and bladder, heart and lungs, kidney and spleen,

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: spit and snot, sweat and fat, blood and synovial fluid, bile and grease.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: Then in nine streams the filth is always flowing. There is muck from the eyes, wax from the ears,

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: and snot from the nostrils. The mouth sometimes vomits bile and sometimes phlegm. And from the body, sweat and waste.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: Then there is the hollow head all filled with brains. Governed by ignorance, the fool thinks it's lovely.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: And when it lies dead, bloated and livid, dumped in a charnel ground, the relatives forget it.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: It's devoured by dogs, by jackals, wolves, and worms. It's devoured by crows and vultures, and any other creatures there.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: A wise mendicant here, having heard the Buddha's words, fully understands it, for they see it as it is.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: "As this is, so is that, as that is, so is this." They'd blanch desire for the body inside and out.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: That wise mendicant here rid of desire and lust, has found the peace free of death, extinguishment, the state that does not pass.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: This two-legged body is dirty and stinking, full of different carcasses, and oozing all over the place— but still it is cherished!

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 1.11 Victory Over Desire for the Body
text: And if, on account of such a body, someone prides themselves or looks down on others— what is that but a failure to see?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Peril stems from intimacy, dust comes from an abode. Freedom from abode and intimacy: that is the sage's vision.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having cut down what's grown, they wouldn't replant, nor would they nurture what's growing. That's who they call a sage wandering alone, the great seer has seen the state of peace.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having appraised the fields and measured the seeds, they wouldn't nurture them with moisture. Truly that sage who sees the ending of rebirth has left speculation behind and is beyond reckoning.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Understanding all the planes of rebirth, not wanting a single one of them; truly that sage freed of greed need not swim, for they have reached the far shore.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The vanquisher of all, knower of all, so very intelligent, unsullied in the midst of all things, has given up all, freed in the ending of craving: that's who the attentive know as a sage.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Strong in wisdom, with precepts and observances intact, serene, loving absorption, mindful, released from chains, kind, undefiled: that's who the attentive know as a sage.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The diligent sage wandering alone, is unshaken by blame and praise— like a lion not startled by sounds, like wind not caught in a net, like water not sticking to a lotus. Leader of others, not by others led: that's who the attentive know as a sage.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Steady as a post in a bathing-place when others speak endlessly against them, freed of greed, with senses stilled: that's who the attentive know as a sage.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Steadfast, straight as a spindle, horrified by wicked deeds, discerning the just and the unjust: that's who the attentive know as a sage.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Restrained, they do no evil, young or middle-aged, the sage is self-controlled. Irreproachable, he does not insult anyone: that's who the attentive know as a sage.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When one who lives on charity receives alms, from the top, the middle, or the leftovers, they think it unworthy to praise or put down: that's who the attentive know as a sage.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The sage lives refraining from sex, even when young is not tied down, refraining from indulgence and negligence, freed: that's who the attentive know as a sage.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Understanding the world, the seer of the ultimate goal, the unaffected one, having crossed the flood and the ocean, has cut the ties, unattached and undefiled: that's who the attentive know as a sage.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The two are not the same, far apart in lifestyle and conduct— the householder providing for a wife, and the selfless one true to their vows. The unrestrained householder kills other creatures, while the restrained sage always protects living creatures.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As the crested blue-necked peacock flying through the sky never approaches the speed of the swan, so the householder cannot compete with the mendicant, the sage meditating secluded in the woods.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Whatever beings have gathered here, on the ground or in the sky: may beings all be of happy heart, and listen carefully to what is said.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So pay heed, all you beings, have love for humankind, who day and night bring offerings; please protect them diligently.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: There's no wealth in this life or the next, no sublime gem in the heavens, that equals the Realized One. This sublime gem is in the Buddha: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Ending, dispassion, the undying, the sublime, attained by the Sakyan Sage immersed in samādhi; there is nothing equal to that Dhamma. This sublime gem is in the Dhamma: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The purity praised by the highest Buddha is said to be the "immersion with immediate fruit"; no equal to that immersion is found. This sublime gem is in the Dhamma: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The eight individual persons praised by the good are the four pairs of the Holy One's disciples; they are worthy of religious donations, what's given to them is very fruitful. This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Dedicated to Gotama's dispensation, strong-minded, free of sense desire, they've attained the goal, plunged into freedom from death, and enjoy the quenching they've freely gained. This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As Indra's pillar rooted in earth is not shaken by the four winds, I say a true person is like this, who sees the noble truths in experience. This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those who fathom the noble truths taught by the one of deep wisdom, do not take an eighth life, even if they are hugely negligent. This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When they attain to vision they give up three things: substantialist view, doubt, and any attachment to precepts and observances.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They're freed from the four places of loss, and cannot do six things. This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Even if they do a bad deed by body, speech, or mind, they are unable to conceal it; this, it's said, is the inability of one who has seen the truth. This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Like a tall forest tree crowned with flowers in the first month of summer; that's how he taught the superb Dhamma, leading to extinguishment, the ultimate benefit. This sublime gem is in the Buddha: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The superb, knower of the superb, giver of the superb, bringer of the superb; taught the superb Dhamma supreme. This sublime gem is in the Buddha: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The old is ended, nothing new is produced; their minds have no desire for future rebirth. Withered are the seeds, there's no desire for growth, those attentive ones are extinguished like this lamp. This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha: by this truth, may you be well!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Whatever beings have gathered here, on the ground or in the sky: the Realized One is honored by gods and humans! We bow to the Buddha! May you be safe!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Whatever beings have gathered here, on the ground or in the sky: the Realized One is honored by gods and humans! We bow to the Dhamma! May you be safe!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Whatever beings have gathered here, on the ground or in the sky: the Realized One is honored by gods and humans! We bow to the Saṅgha! May you be safe!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The good eat properly obtained millet, wild grains, broomcorn, greens, tubers, and grapes. They don't lie to get what they want.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But when you eat delicious food, nicely cooked and prepared, and offered by others, enjoying a dish of fine rice, Kassapa, you eat putrefaction.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'Putrefaction is not appropriate for me'— so you said, O brahmin only by kin. Yet here you are enjoying a dish of fine rice, well prepared with the flesh of fowl. I'm asking you this, Kassapa: what do you take to be putrefaction?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Killing creatures, mutilation, murder, abduction; stealing, lying, cheating and fraud, learning crooked spells, adultery: this is putrefaction, not eating meat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: People here with unbridled sensuality, greedy for tastes, mixed up in impurity, nihilists, immoral, intractable: this is putrefaction, not eating meat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Tough, callous calumniators, pitiless and arrogant betrayers of friends, misers who never give anything: this is putrefaction, not eating meat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Anger, vanity, obstinacy, contrariness, deceit, jealousy, boastfulness, haughtiness, intimacy with the wicked: this is putrefaction, not eating meat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The ill-behaved, debt-evaders, informants, business cheats and con-artists, vile men committing sin: this is putrefaction, not eating meat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: People here who can't stop harming living creatures, taking from others, intent on hurting, immoral, cruel, harsh, lacking regard for others: this is putrefaction, not eating meat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Greedy, hostile, aggressive to others, and addicted to evil—those beings pass into darkness, falling headlong into hell: this is putrefaction, not eating meat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not fish or flesh or fasting, nudity or baldness, or dreadlocks or dirt, not rough hides or serving the sacred flame, or the many endless mortifications in the world, not hymns or oblations, sacrifices or seasonal observances, will cleanse a mortal not free of doubt.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Guarding the streams of sense impressions, wander with faculties understood, standing on the teaching, delighting in integrity and tenderness. The attentive have slipped their chains and given up all suffering; they don't cling to the seen and the heard."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The Buddha explained this matter to him again and again, until the master of hymns understood it. It was illustrated with colorful verses by the sage free of putrefaction, unattached, hard to trace.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having heard the fine words of the Buddha, that are free of putrefaction, casting aside all suffering; humbled, he bowed to the Realized One, and right away begged to go forth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Flouting conscience, loathing it, saying "I'm on your side", but not following up in deeds— know they're not on your side.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Some say nice things to their friends without following it up. The wise will recognize one who talks without doing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: No true friend relentlessly suspects betrayal, looking for fault. One on whom you rest, like a child on the breast, is a true friend, not split from you by others.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One whose reward is the fruit of bearing the burden of service develops a happy state, producing joy and attracting praise.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One who has drunk the nectar of seclusion and the nectar of peace, free of stress, free of evil, drinks the joyous nectar of Dhamma.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta's Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. That deity addressed the Buddha in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Many gods and humans have thought about blessings desiring well-being: declare the highest blessing."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Not to fraternize with fools, but to fraternize with the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor: this is the highest blessing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Living in a suitable region, having made merit in the past, being rightly resolved in oneself, this is the highest blessing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Education and a craft, discipline and training, and well-spoken speech: this is the highest blessing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Caring for mother and father, kindness to children and partners, and unstressful work: this is the highest blessing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Giving and righteous conduct, kindness to relatives, blameless deeds: this is the highest blessing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Desisting and abstaining from evil, avoiding drinking liquor, diligence in good qualities: this is the highest blessing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Respect and placidity, contentment and gratitude, and timely listening to the teaching: this is the highest blessing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Patience, being easy to admonish, the sight of ascetics, and timely discussion of the teaching: this is the highest blessing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Fervor and chastity seeing the noble truths, and realization of extinguishment: this is the highest blessing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Though touched by worldly conditions, their mind does not tremble; sorrowless, stainless, secure: this is the highest blessing.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having completed these things, undefeated everywhere; everywhere they go in safety: this is their highest blessing."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Gayā on the cut-stone ledge in the haunt of Spiky the native spirit. Now at that time the native spirits Shaggy and Spiky were passing by not far from the Buddha. So Shaggy said to Spiky, "That's an ascetic." "That's no ascetic, he's a faker! I'll soon find out whether he's an ascetic or a faker."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Spiky went up to the Buddha and leaned up against his body, but the Buddha pulled away. Then Spiky said to the Buddha, "Are you afraid, ascetic?" "No, respectable sir, I'm not afraid. But your touch is nasty."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I will ask you a question, ascetic. If you don't answer me, I'll drive you insane, or explode your heart, or grab you by the feet and throw you to the far shore of the Ganges!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I don't see anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans who could do that to me. But anyway, ask what you wish." Then Spiky addressed the Buddha in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Where do greed and hate come from? From where spring discontent, desire, and terror? Where do the mind's thoughts originate, like a crow let loose by boys."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Greed and hate come from here; from here spring discontent, desire, and terror; here's where the mind's thoughts originate, like a crow let loose by boys.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Born of affection, originating in oneself, like prop roots sprouting from a banyan; the many kinds of attachment to sensual pleasures are like camel's foot creeper creeping through the woods.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those who understand where they come from dispel them—listen up, spirit! They cross this flood so hard to cross, not crossed before, so as to not be reborn."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A righteous life, a spiritual life, they call this the supreme treasure. But if someone goes forth from the lay life to homelessness

author: Gotama Buddha
text: who is of scurrilous character, a beast and a bully, their life gets worse, as poison grows inside them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A mendicant who loves to quarrel, wrapped in delusion, doesn't even know what's been explained in the Dhamma taught by the Buddha.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Harassing those who are evolved, governed by ignorance, they don't know that corruption is the path that leads to hell.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Entering the underworld, passing from womb to womb, from darkness to darkness, such a mendicant falls into suffering after death.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One such as that is like a sewer brimful with years of filth for it's hard to clean one full of grime.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Mendicants, knowing that someone is like this, attached to the domestic life, of corrupt wishes and wicked intent, of bad behavior and alms-resort,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: then having gathered in harmony, you should expel them. Throw out the trash! Get rid of the rubbish!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And sweep away the scraps— they're not ascetics, they just think they are. When you've thrown out those of corrupt wishes, of bad behavior and alms-resort,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: dwell in communion, ever mindful, the pure with the pure. Then in harmony, alert, you'll make an end of suffering.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then several old and well-to-do brahmins of Kosala—elderly and senior, who were advanced in years and had reached the final stage of life—went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to the Buddha: "Worthy Gotama, are the ancient principles of the brahmins exhibited these days among brahmins?" "No, brahmins, they are not." "If you wouldn't mind, Worthy Gotama, please teach us the ancient principles of the brahmins." "Well then, brahmins, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak." "Yes, worthy sir," they replied. The Buddha said this:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The ancient seers used to be restrained and austere. Having given up the five sensual stimuli, they lived for their own true good.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Brahmins used to own no cattle, nor gold coin or grain. Chanting was their money and grain, which they guarded as a gift from god.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Food was prepared for them and left beside their doors. People believed that food prepared in faith should be given to them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: With colorful clothes, lodgings and houses, prosperous nations and countries honored those brahmins.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Brahmins used to be inviolable and invincible, protected by principle. No one ever turned them away from the doors of families.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For forty-eight years they led the spiritual life. The brahmins of old pursued their quest for knowledge and conduct.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Brahmins never transgressed with another, nor did they purchase a wife. They lived together in love, joining together by mutual consent.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Brahmins never approached their wives for sex during the time outside the fertile phase of the menstrual cycle after menstruation.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They praised chastity and morality, integrity, tenderness, and fervor, gentleness and harmlessness, and also patience.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He who was supreme among them, godlike, staunchly vigorous, did not engage in sex even in a dream.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Training in line with their duties, many smart people here praised chastity and morality, and also patience.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They begged for rice, bedding, clothes, ghee, and oil. Having collected them legitimately, they arranged a sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But they slew no cows while serving at the sacrifice. Like a mother, father, or brother, or some other relative, cows are our best friends, the fonts of medicine.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They give food and strength, and beauty and happiness. Knowing these benefits, they slew no cows.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The brahmins were delicate and tall, beautiful and glorious. They were keen on all the duties according to their teachings. So long as they continued in the world, people flourished happily.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But perversion crept into them little by little when they saw the transformation of the king and the ladies in all their finery.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Their chariots were harnessed with thoroughbreds, well-made with bright canopies, and their homes and houses were neatly divided section by section.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They were lavished with herds of cattle, and furnished with bevies of lovely ladies. This extravagant human wealth was coveted by the brahmins.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They compiled hymns to that end, approached King Okkāka and said, 'You have plenty of money and grain. Sacrifice! For you have much treasure. Sacrifice! For you have much money.'

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Persuaded by the brahmins, the king, chief of charioteers, performed horse sacrifice, human sacrifice, the sacrifices of the 'casting of the yoke-pin', the 'royal soma drinking', and the 'unimpeded'. When he had carried out these sacrifices, he gave riches to the brahmins.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: There were cattle, bedding, and clothes, and ladies in all their finery; chariots harnessed with thoroughbreds, well-made with bright canopies;

author: Gotama Buddha
text: and lovely homes, nicely divided section by section. Having furnished them with different grains, he gave riches to the brahmins.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When they got hold of that wealth, they arranged to store it up. Falling under the sway of desire, their craving grew and grew. They compiled hymns to that end, approached King Okkāka once more and said,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'Like water and earth, gold coin, riches, and grain, are cows for humankind, as they are essential for creatures. Sacrifice! For you have much treasure. Sacrifice! For you have much money.'

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Persuaded by the brahmins, the king, chief of charioteers, had many hundred thousand cows slain at the sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Neither with feet nor with horns do cows harm anyone at all. Cows meek as lambs supply buckets of milk. But taking them by the horns, the king slew them with a sword.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: At that the gods and the ancestors, with Indra, the titans and monsters, roared out: 'This is a crime against nature!' as the sword fell on the cows.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: There used to be three kinds of illness: greed, starvation, and old age. But due to the slaughter of cows, this grew to be ninety-eight.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: This crime of the rods is of ancient descent. Killing innocent creatures, the sacrificers forsake righteousness.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And that is how this mean old practice was criticized by sensible people. Wherever they see such a thing, folk criticize the sacrificer.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: With righteousness gone, peasants and menials were split, as were many aristocrats, and wives looked down on their husbands.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Aristocrats and brahmins only by kin, and others protected by their clan, neglecting their genealogy, fell under the sway of sensual pleasures."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When he had spoken, those well-to-do brahmins said to the Buddha, "Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! … From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If you would learn the teaching from someone, honor them as the gods honor Indra. Then they will have confidence in you, and being learned, they reveal the teaching.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Heeding well, an attentive one, practicing in line with that teaching grows intelligent, discerning, and subtle through diligently sticking close to such a person.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But associating with a petty fool who falls short of the goal, jealous, then unable to discern the teaching in this life, one proceeds to death still plagued by doubts.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: It's like a man who has plunged into a river, a rushing torrent in spate. As they are swept away downstream, how could they help others across?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Just so, one unable to discern the teaching, who hasn't studied the meaning under the learned, not knowing it oneself, still plagued by doubts, how could they help others to contemplate?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But one who has embarked on a strong boat equipped with rudder and oar, would bring many others across there with skill, care, and thoughtfulness.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So too one who understands—a knowledge master, evolved, learned, and unflappable— can help others to contemplate, so long as they are prepared to listen carefully.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That's why you should spend time with a true person, intelligent and learned. Having understood the meaning, putting it into practice, one who understands the teaching would find happiness.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "With what morality, what conduct, fostering what deeds, would a person lay the foundations right, and reach the highest goal?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Honoring elders without jealousy, they'd know the time to visit their respected teachers. Treasuring the chance for a Dhamma talk, they'd listen carefully to the well-spoken words.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: At the right time, they'd enter the vicinity of their respected teachers in placid manner, leaving obstinacy behind. They'd call to mind and put into practice the meaning, the teaching, self-control, and the spiritual life.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Delighting in the teaching, enjoying the teaching, standing on the teaching, evaluating the teaching, they'd never say anything that degraded the teaching, but would be guided by genuine words well-spoken.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Giving up mirth, muttered prayer, weeping, ill will, deceit, fawning, greed, conceit, aggression, crudeness, stains, and indulgence, they'd wander free of vanity, steadfast.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Understanding is the essence of well-spoken words, stillness is the essence of learning and understanding. Wisdom and learning do not flourish in a hasty and negligent person.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those happy with the teaching proclaimed by the Noble One are supreme in speech, mind, and deed. Abiding in peace, gentleness, and stillness, they've realized the essence of learning and wisdom."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Get up and meditate! What's the point in your sleeping? How can the afflicted slumber when inflicted by an arrow strike?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Get up and meditate! Train hard for peace! The King of Death has caught you heedless— don't let him fool you under his sway.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Needy gods and humans are held back by clinging: get over it. Don't let the moment pass you by. For if you miss your moment you'll grieve when sent to hell.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Negligence is always dust; dust follows right behind negligence. Through diligence and knowledge, pluck out the dart from yourself.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Does familiarity breed contempt, even for the man of wisdom? Do you honor he who holds aloft the torch for all humanity?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Familiarity breeds no contempt for the man of wisdom. I always honor he who holds aloft the torch for all humanity."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "One who's given up the five sensual stimulations, so pleasing and delightful, and who's left the home life out of faith— let them make an end to suffering!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Mix with spiritual friends, stay in remote lodgings, secluded and quiet, and eat in moderation.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Robes, almsfood, requisites and lodgings: don't crave such things; don't come back to this world again.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Be restrained in the monastic code and the five sense faculties. With mindfulness immersed in the body, be full of disillusionment.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Turn away from the sign that's attractive, provoking lust. With mind unified and serene, meditate on the ugly aspects of the body.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Meditate on the signless, give up the tendency to conceit; and when you comprehend conceit, you will live at peace."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That is how the Buddha regularly advised Venerable Rāhula with these verses.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Āḷavī, at Āḷavī's premier shrine. Now at that time it was not long after Venerable Vaṅgīsa's mentor, the senior monk named Nigrodhakappa, had become fully quenched. Then as Vaṅgīsa was in private retreat this thought came to his mind: "Has my mentor become quenched or not?" Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Vaṅgīsa came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him: "Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind. 'Has my mentor become quenched or not?'" Then Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I ask the Teacher unrivaled in wisdom, who has cut off all doubts in this very life: a monk has died at Āḷavī's premier shrine, who was well-known, famous, and quenched.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Nigrodhakappa was his name; it was given to that brahmin by you, Blessed One. He wandered in your honor, yearning for freedom, energetic, a resolute Seer of Truth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: O Sakyan, All-seer, we all wish to know about that disciple. Our ears are eager to hear, for you are the most excellent teacher.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Cut off our doubt, declare this to us; your wisdom is vast, tell us of his quenching! All-seer, speak among us, like the thousand-eyed Sakka in the midst of the gods!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Whatever ties there are, or paths to delusion, or things on the side of unknowing, or that are bases of doubt vanish on reaching a Realized One, for his eye is the best of all people's.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If no man were ever to disperse corruptions, like the wind dispersing the stormclouds, darkness would shroud the whole world; not even brilliant men would shine.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The attentive are bringers of light; my hero, that is what I think of you. We've come for your discernment and knowledge: here in this assembly, declare to us about Kappāyana.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Swiftly send forth your sweet, sweet voice, like a goose stretching its neck, gently honking, lucid-flowing, with lovely tone: alert, we all listen to you.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You have entirely abandoned birth and death; curbed and pure, I urge you, speak the Dhamma! For ordinary people have no wish-granter, but Realized Ones have a comprehensibility-granter.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Your answer is definitive, and we will adopt it, for you have perfect understanding. We raise our cupped palms one last time, one of unrivaled wisdom, don't deliberately confuse us.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing the teaching of the noble ones from top to bottom, one of unrivaled energy, don't deliberately confuse us. As a man baking in the summer sun would long for water, I long for your voice, so let the sound rain forth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Surely Kappāyana did not lead the spiritual life in vain? Did he realize quenching, or did he still have a residue? Let us hear what kind of liberation he had!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "He cut off craving for name and form right here," said the Buddha, "the river of darkness that had long lain within him. He has entirely crossed over birth and death." So declared the Blessed One, the leader of the five.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Now that I have heard your words, seventh of seers, I am confident. My question, it seems, was not in vain, the brahmin did not deceive me.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As he said, so he did— he was a disciple of the Buddha. He cut the net of death the deceiver, so extended and strong.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Blessed One, Kappāyana saw the starting point of grasping. He has indeed gone far beyond Death's dominion so hard to pass."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I ask the sage abounding in wisdom— crossed-over, gone beyond, quenched, steadfast: when a mendicant has left home, casting aside sensuality, what's the right way to wander the world?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "When they've eradicated superstitions," said the Buddha, "about celestial portents, dreams, or bodily marks; with the stain of superstitions left behind, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A mendicant ought dispel desire for pleasures human or heavenly; with rebirth transcended and truth comprehended, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Putting backbiting behind them, a mendicant gives up anger and stinginess; with favoring and opposing left behind, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When the loved and the unloved are both left behind, not grasping or dependent on anything; freed from all things that fetter, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Finding no core in attachments, rid of desire for things they've acquired, independent, needing no one to guide them, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not hostile in speech, mind, or deed, they've rightly understood the teaching. Aspiring to the state of extinguishment, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not gloating that, 'they bow to me'; though reviled, they'd still stay in touch; not besotted when getting food from others, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When greed and craving to live again are cast off, a mendicant refrains from violence and abduction; rid of indecision, free of thorns, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing what is suitable for themselves, a mendicant would hurt no one in the world; understanding the teaching in line with the truth, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have no underlying tendencies at all, and are rid of unskillful roots; free of hope, with no need for hope, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Defilements ended, conceit given up, beyond all manner of desire; tamed, quenched, and steadfast, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Faithful, learned, seer of the sure path, an attentive one joins no faction among sects; rid of greed, hate, and aversion, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A purified victor with veil cast off, among worldly things master, transcendent, stilled; expert in knowledge of conditions' cessation, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They're over speculating on the future or past, and understand what it means to be pure; freed from all the sense fields, they'd rightly wander the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The state of peace is understood, the truth is comprehended, they've openly seen defilements cast off; and with the ending of all attachments, they'd rightly wander the world."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Clearly, Blessed One, it is just as you say. One who lives like this is a tamed mendicant, passed beyond all fetters and yokes: they'd rightly wander the world."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then the lay follower Dhammika, together with five hundred lay followers, went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and addressed him in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I ask you, Gotama, whose wisdom is vast: what does one do to become a good disciple, both one who has left the home, and the lay followers staying at home?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For you understand the course and destiny of the world with all its gods. There is no equal to you who sees the subtle meaning, for you are the Buddha most excellent, they say.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having experienced all knowledge, you reveal the teaching out of sympathy for beings. All-seer, you have cast off the veil, and immaculate, you dazzle the whole world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The dragon king Erāvaṇa, hearing you called 'Victor', came into your presence. He consulted with you then, having heard your words, left consoled, saying 'Excellent!'

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And King Kuvera Vessavaṇa also approached to ask about the teaching. You also answered him, O attentive one, and hearing you he too was consoled.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those monastics of other religions given to debate, whether Ājīvakas or Jains, all fail to overtake you in wisdom, like a standing man next to a sprinter.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those brahmins given to debate, some of whom are quite senior, all end up beholden to you for the meaning, and others too who think themselves debaters.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So subtle and pleasant is the teaching that is well proclaimed by you, Blessed One. It's all we long to hear. So when asked, O Best of Buddhas, tell us!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: All these mendicants have gathered, and the layfolk too are here to listen. Let them hear the teaching the immaculate one discovered, like gods listening to the fine words of Vāsava."

author: Gotama Buddha
