text: "Listen to me, mendicants, I will educate you in the cleansing teaching; all bear it in mind. A thoughtful person, seeing the meaning, would adopt the deportment proper to a renunciate.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: No way would a mendicant go out at the wrong time; at the right time, they'd walk the village for alms. For chains bind one who wanders at the wrong time, which is why the Buddhas avoid it.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Sights, sounds, tastes, smells, and touches, which drive beings mad— dispel desire for such things, and enter for the morning meal at the right time.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: After receiving alms for the day, on returning a mendicant would sit in private alone. Inwardly reflective, they'd curb their mind from outside things, keeping themselves collected.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Should they converse with a disciple, with anyone else, or with a mendicant, they'd bring up only the sublime teaching, not dividing or blaming.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For some contend in debate, but we praise not those of little wisdom. In place after place they are bound in chains, for they send their mind over there far away.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Alms, a dwelling, a bed and seat, and water for rinsing the dust from the cloak— after hearing the teaching of the Holy One, a disciple of outstanding wisdom would use these after appraisal.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That's why, when it comes to alms and lodgings, and water for rinsing the dust from the cloak, a mendicant is unsullied in the midst of these things, like a droplet on a lotus-leaf.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Now I shall tell you the householder's duty, doing which one becomes a good disciple. For one burdened with possessions does not get to realize the whole of the mendicant's practice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They'd not kill any creature, nor have them killed, nor grant permission for others to kill. They've laid aside violence toward all creatures frail or firm that there are in the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Next, a disciple would avoid knowingly taking anything not given at all, they'd not get others to do it, nor grant them permission to steal; they'd avoid all theft.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A sensible person would avoid the unchaste life, like a burning pit of coals. But if unable to remain chaste, they'd not transgress with another's partner.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: In a council or assembly, or one on one, they would not lie. They'd not get others to lie, nor grant them permission to lie; they'd avoid all untruths.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A householder espousing this teaching would not consume liquor or drink. They'd not get others to drink, nor grant them permission to drink; knowing that ends in intoxication.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For drunken fools do bad things, and encourage other heedless folk. Shun this field of demerit, the maddening, deluding frolic of fools.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You shouldn't kill living creatures, or steal, or lie, or drink liquor. Be chaste, refraining from sex, and don't eat at night, the wrong time.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not wearing garlands or applying fragrance, you should sleep on a low bed, or a mat on the ground. This is the eight-factored sabbath, they say, revealed by the Buddha, who has gone to suffering's end.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then having rightly undertaken the sabbath complete in all its eight factors on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight, as well as on the fortnightly special displays,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: at daybreak after the sabbath a clever person, rejoicing with confident heart, would distribute food and drink to the mendicant Saṅgha as is fitting.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One should rightfully support one's parents, and undertake a legitimate business. A diligent layperson observing these duties ascends to the gods named 'self-radiant'."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I shall extol going forth with the example of the Clear-eyed One, the course of inquiry that led to his choice to go forth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'This life at home is cramped, a realm of dirt.' 'The life of one gone forth is like an open space.' Seeing this, he went forth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having gone forth, he shunned bad deeds of body. And leaving verbal misconduct behind, he purified his livelihood.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The Buddha went to Rājagaha, the Mountainfold of the Magadhans. He betook himself for alms, replete with excellent marks.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Bimbisāra saw him while standing atop his longhouse. Noticing that he was endowed with marks, he said the following:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'Pay heed, sirs, to this one, handsome, majestic, radiant; accomplished in deportment, he looks just a plough's length in front.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Eyes downcast, mindful, unlike one from a low family. Let the king's messengers run out, and find where the mendicant will go.'

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The messengers sent out followed right behind, thinking 'Where will the mendicant go? Where shall he find a place to stay?'

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Wandering indiscriminately for alms, sense doors guarded and well restrained, aware and mindful, his bowl was quickly filled.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having wandered for alms, the sage left the city. He betook himself to Mount Paṇḍava, thinking, 'Here is the place I shall stay.'

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Seeing that he had arrived at a place to stay, the messengers withdrew nearby, but one of them returned to inform the king.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'Great king, the mendicant is on the east flank of Mount Paṇḍava. There he sits, like a tiger or a bull, like a lion in a mountain cave.'

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Hearing the messenger's report, the aristocrat set out hurriedly in his fine chariot toward Mount Paṇḍava.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He went as far as vehicles could go, then dismounted from his chariot, approached on foot, and reaching him, drew near.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Seated, the king greeted him and made polite conversation. When the courtesies were over, he said the following:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'You are young, just a youth, a lad in the prime of life. You are endowed with beauty and stature, like an aristocrat of good birth

author: Gotama Buddha
text: in glory at the army's head, surrounded by a troop of elephants. I offer you pleasures—enjoy them! But please tell me of your birth.'

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'Up north, O King, on the slopes of the Himalayas, full of wealth and strength, lies the land of one whose abode is among the Kosalans.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Their clan is named for the Sun, they are Sakyans by birth. I have gone forth from that family— I do not yearn for sensual pleasure.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, seeing renunciation as sanctuary, I shall go on to strive; that is where my mind delights.'"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "During my time of resolute striving back on the bank of the Nerañjara River, I was meditating very hard for the sake of sanctuary from the yoke.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Namucī approached, speaking words of kindness: 'You're thin, discolored, on the verge of death.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Death has a thousand parts of you, one fraction is left to life. Live, worthy sir! Life is better! Living, you can make merits.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: While leading the spiritual life and serving the sacred flame, you can pile up abundant merit— so what will striving do for you?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Hard to walk is the path of striving, hard to do, a hard challenge to win.'" These are the verses Māra spoke as he stood beside the Buddha.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When Māra had spoken in this way, the Buddha said this: "O Wicked One, kinsman of the negligent, you're here for your own purpose.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: I have no need for the slightest bit of merit. Those with need for merit are fit for Māra to address.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: I have faith and energy too, and wisdom is found in me. When I am so resolute, why do you beg me to live?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The rivers and streams might be dried by the wind, so why, when I am resolute, should it not dry up my blood?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And while the blood is drying up, the bile and phlegm dry too. And as my muscles waste away, my mind grows more serene. And all the stronger grow mindfulness and wisdom and immersion.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As I meditate like this, having attained the supreme feeling, my mind has no interest in sensual pleasures: behold a being's purity!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Sensual pleasures are your first army, the second is called discontent, hunger and thirst are the third, and the fourth is said to be craving.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Your fifth is dullness and drowsiness, the sixth is said to be cowardice, your seventh is doubt, contempt and obstinacy are your eighth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Profit, praise, and honor, and misbegotten fame; the extolling of oneself while scorning others.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: This is your army, Namucī, the strike force of the Dark One. Only a hero can defeat it, but in victory there lies bliss.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Let me gird myself— curse my life! I'd rather die in battle than live on in defeat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Here some ascetics and brahmins are swallowed up, not to be seen again. And they do not know the path traveled by those true to their vows.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Seeing Māra ready with his legions, surrounded by his bannered forces, I shall meet them in battle— they'll never make me retreat!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That army of yours has never been beaten by the world with all its gods. Yet I shall smash it with wisdom, like an unfired pot with a stone.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having brought my thoughts under control, and established mindfulness well, I shall wander from nation to nation, guiding many disciples.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Diligent and resolute, following my instructions, they will proceed despite your will, to where there is no sorrow."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "For seven years I followed step by step behind the Blessed One. I found no vulnerability in the mindful Awakened One.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A crow once circled a stone that looked like a lump of fat. 'Perhaps I'll find something tender,' it thought, 'perhaps there's something tasty.'

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But finding nothing tasty, the crow left that place. Like the crow that pecked the stone, I leave Gotama disappointed."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So stricken with sorrow that his harp dropped from his armpit, that spirit, downcast, vanished right there.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants, "Mendicants!" "Venerable sir," they replied. The Buddha said this:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Mendicants, speech that has four factors is well spoken, not poorly spoken. It's blameless and is not criticized by sensible people. What four? It's when a mendicant speaks well, not poorly; their speech is principled, not unprincipled; they speak pleasantly, not unpleasantly; and they speak truthfully, not falsely. Speech with these four factors is well spoken, not poorly spoken. It's blameless and is not criticized by sensible people." That is what the Buddha said. Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Good people say well-spoken words are foremost; second, speech ought be principled, not unprincipled; third, speak pleasantly, not unpleasantly; and fourth, speak truthfully, not falsely."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said, "I feel inspired to speak, Blessed One! I feel inspired to speak, Holy One!" "Then speak as you feel inspired," said the Buddha. Then Vaṅgīsa extolled the Buddha in his presence with fitting verses:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Speak only those words that do not hurt yourself nor harm others; such speech is truly well spoken.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Speak only pleasing words, words gladly welcomed. Pleasing words are those that bring nothing bad to others.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Truth itself is undying speech: this is an ancient teaching. Good people say the teaching and meaning are grounded in truth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The words spoken by the Buddha for finding the sanctuary, extinguishment, for making an end of suffering, this really is the best kind of speech."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the Kosalan lands on the bank of the Sundarikā River. Now at that time the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā was serving the sacred flame and performing the fire sacrifice on the bank of the Sundarikā. Then he rose from his seat and surveyed the four quarters, wondering, "Now who might eat the leftovers of this oblation?" He saw the Buddha meditating at the root of a certain tree with his robe pulled over his head. Taking the leftovers of the oblation in his left hand and a pitcher in the right he approached the Buddha.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: When he heard Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā's footsteps the Buddha uncovered his head. Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā thought, "This man is shaven, he is shaven!" And he wanted to turn back. But he thought, "Even some brahmins are shaven. Why don't I go to him and ask about his birth?" Then the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā went up to the Buddha, and said to him, "Sir, what are you by birth?"

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Then the Buddha addressed Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "I am no brahmin, nor am I a ruler, nor peasant nor anything else. Fully understanding the clan of ordinary people, I wander in the world owning nothing, reflective.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Clad in my cloak, I wander without home, my hair shorn, quenched. Since I'm unburdened by sons of Manu, it's inappropriate to ask me about clan."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "Actually sir, when brahmins meet they politely ask each other whether they are brahmins."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "Well, if you say that you're a brahmin, and that I am not, I shall question you on that Sāvitrī Prayer, with its three lines and twenty-four syllables."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "On what grounds have seers and men, aristocrats and brahmins here in the world performed so many different sacrifices to the gods?"

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "During a sacrifice, should a past-master, a knowledge master, receive an oblation, it profits the donor, I say."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "Then clearly my oblation will be profitable," said the brahmin, "since I have met such a knowledge master. It's because I'd never met anyone like you that others ate the sacrificial cake."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "So then, brahmin, since you have approached me as a seeker of the good, ask. Perhaps you may find here someone intelligent, peaceful, unclouded, untroubled, with no need for hope."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "Worthy Gotama, I like to sacrifice and wish to perform a sacrifice. Please advise me, for I do not understand where an oblation is profitable; tell me this."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "Well then, brahmin, listen up, I will teach you the Dhamma.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Don't ask about birth, ask about conduct; for the fire of Jātaveda is born from sticks. A steadfast sage, even though from a low class family, is a thoroughbred checked by conscience.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Tamed by truth, fulfilled by taming, a complete knowledge master who has completed the spiritual journey— that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Those who have left sensuality behind, wandering homeless, self-controlled, straight as a shuttle— that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Those freed of greed, with senses stilled, like the moon released from the eclipse— that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: They wander the world unobstructed, always mindful, calling nothing their own— that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Having left sensuality behind, wandering triumphant, knowing the end of rebirth and death, quenched and cool as a lake: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Good among the good, far from the bad, the Realized One has infinite wisdom. Unsullied in this life and the next: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: In whom dwells no deceit or conceit, rid of greed, unselfish, with no need for hope, with anger cast aside, quenched, a brahmin rid of sorrow's stain: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: He has given up the mind's home, and has no possessions at all. Not grasping to this life or the next: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Serene, he has crossed the flood, and has understood the teaching with ultimate view. With defilements ended, bearing his final body: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: In whom desire to be reborn, and caustic speech are cleared and ended, and are no more; that knowledge master, everywhere free: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: He has slipped his chains, he's chained no more, among those caught in conceit he is free of conceit; he has fully understood suffering with its field and ground: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Not relying on hope, seeing seclusion, well past the views proclaimed by others. In him there are no supporting conditions at all: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: He has comprehended all things, high and low, cleared them and ended them, so they are no more. Peaceful, freed in the ending of grasping: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: He sees the ending of rebirth's fetter, and has cast aside all manner of desire. Pure, stainless, immaculate, flawless: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Not seeing himself in terms of a self, he is stilled, sincere, and steadfast. Imperturbable, kind, wishless: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: He harbors no delusions within at all, he has insight into all things. He bears his final body, attained to the state of grace, the supreme awakening. That's how the purity of a spirit is defined: the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "Let my oblation be a true offering, since I have found such a knowledge master! I see divinity in person! Accept my offering, Blessed One: please eat my sacrificial cake."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "Food enchanted by a verse isn't fit for me to eat. That's not the principle of those who see, brahmin. The Buddhas cast aside things enchanted with verses. Since there is such a principle, brahmin, that's how they live.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Serve with other food and drink the consummate one, the great seer, with defilements ended and remorse stilled. For he is the field for the seeker of merit."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "Please, Blessed One, help me understand: now that I have found your teaching, when I look for someone during a sacrifice, who should eat the religious donation of one like me?"

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "One who is rid of aggression, whose mind is unclouded, who is liberated from sensual pleasures, and who has cast aside dullness.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: One who has erased perimeters and limits, expert in birth and death, a sage, blessed with sagacity. When such a person comes to the sacrifice,

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: get rid of your scowl! Honor them with cupped palms, and venerate them with food and drink, and in this way your religious donation will succeed."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: "The Buddha is worthy of the sacrificial cake, he is the supreme field of merit, recipient of gifts from the whole world; what's given to the worthy one is very fruitful."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 3.4 With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake
text: Then the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā said to the Buddha, "Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what's there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways. I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha. May I receive the going forth, the ordination in the worthy Gotama's presence?" And the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha's presence. And soon after, he became one of the perfected.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture's Peak Mountain. Then the student Māgha approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side, and said to the Buddha:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I'm a giver, worthy Gotama, a donor; I am bountiful and committed to charity. I seek wealth in a principled manner, and with that legitimate wealth I give to one person, to two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred people or even more. Giving and sacrificing like this, worthy Gotama, do I brim with much merit?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Indeed you do, student. A giver or donor who is bountiful and committed to charity, who seeks wealth in a principled manner, and with that legitimate wealth gives to one person, or up to a hundred people or even more, brims with much merit." Then Māgha addressed the Buddha in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I ask the bountiful Gotama," said Māgha, "wearing an ochre robe, wandering homeless. Suppose a lay donor who is committed to charity makes a sacrifice seeking merit, looking for merit, giving food and drink to others here: how is their offering purified?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Suppose a lay donor who is committed to charity," replied the Buddha, "makes a sacrifice seeking merit, looking for merit, giving food and drink to others here: such a one would succeed due to those who are worthy of donations."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Suppose a lay donor who is committed to charity," said Māgha, "makes a sacrifice seeking merit, looking for merit, giving food and drink to others here: explain to me who is worthy of donations."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Those who wander the world unattached, consummate, self-controlled, owning nothing: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those who have cut off all fetters and bonds, tamed, liberated, untroubled, with no need for hope: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those who are released from all fetters, tamed, liberated, untroubled, with no need for hope: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having given up greed, hate, and delusion, with defilements ended, the spiritual journey completed: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those in whom dwells no deceit or conceit, with defilements ended, the spiritual journey completed: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those rid of greed, unselfish, with no need for hope, with defilements ended, the spiritual journey completed: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those not fallen prey to cravings, who, having crossed the flood, live unselfishly: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those with no craving at all in the world for any state of existence in this life or the next: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those who have left sensuality behind, wandering homeless, self-controlled, straight as a shuttle: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those freed of greed, with senses stilled, like the moon released from the eclipse: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those assuaged ones free of greed and anger, for whom there are no destinies, being rid of them in this life: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've given up rebirth and death completely, and have gone beyond all indecision: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those who live as their own island, everywhere free, owning nothing: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those here who know this to be true: 'This is my last life, there are no future lives': that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A knowledge master, loving absorption, mindful, who has reached awakening and is a refuge for many: that is where a brahmin seeking merit should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Clearly my questions were not in vain!" said Māgha, "The Buddha has explained to me who is worthy of donations. You are the one here who knows this to be true, for truly you understand this matter.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Suppose a lay donor who is committed to charity makes a sacrifice seeking merit, looking for merit, giving food and drink to others here: explain to me how to accomplish the sacrifice."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Sacrifice, and while doing so," replied the Buddha, "be clear and confident in every way. Sacrifice is the ground standing upon which the sacrificer sheds their flaws.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One free of greed, rid of anger, developing a heart of limitless love, spreads that limitlessness in every direction, ever diligent day and night."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Who is purified, freed, awake? How can one go to the realm of divinity oneself? I do not know, so please tell me when asked, for the Buddha is the divinity I see in person today! To us you are truly the equal of divinity. Brilliant One, how is one reborn in the realm of divinity?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "One who accomplishes the sacrifice with three modes," replied the Buddha, "such a one would succeed due to those who are worthy of donations. Sacrificing like this, one rightly committed to charity is reborn in the realm of divinity, I say."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When he had spoken, the student Māgha said to the Buddha, "Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! … From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground. Now at that time the wanderer Sabhiya had been presented with several questions by a deity who was a former blood relation, saying: "Sabhiya, you should live the spiritual life with whatever ascetic or brahmin answers these questions."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Sabhiya, after learning those questions in the presence of that deity, approached those ascetics and brahmins who led an order and a community, and taught a community, who were well-known and famous religious founders, deemed holy by many people. That is, Pūraṇa Kassapa, the bamboo-staffed ascetic Gosāla, Ajita of the hair blanket, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, and the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan. And he asked them those questions, but they were stumped by them. Displaying annoyance, hate, and bitterness, they questioned Sabhiya in return.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Sabhiya thought, "Those famous ascetics and brahmins were stumped by my questions. Displaying annoyance, hate, and bitterness, they questioned me in return on that matter. Why don't I return to a lesser life so I can enjoy sensual pleasures?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Sabhiya thought, "This ascetic Gotama also leads an order and a community, and tutors a community. He's a well-known and famous religious founder, deemed holy by many people. Why don't I ask him these questions?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then he thought, "Even those ascetics and brahmins who are elderly and senior, who are advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life; who are senior, long standing, long gone forth; who lead an order and a community, and tutor a community; who are well-known and famous religious founders, deemed holy by many people—that is Pūraṇa Kassapa and the rest— were stumped by my questions. They displayed annoyance, hate, and bitterness, and even questioned me in return. How can the ascetic Gotama possibly answer my questions, since he is so young in age and newly gone forth?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then he thought, "An ascetic should not be looked down upon or disparaged because they are young. Though young, the ascetic Gotama has great psychic power and might. Why don't I ask him these questions?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Sabhiya set out for Rājagaha. Traveling stage by stage, he came to Rājagaha, the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground. He went up to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side, and addressed the Buddha in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I've come full of doubts and uncertainties," said Sabhiya, "wishing to ask some questions. Please solve them for me. Answer my questions in turn, in accordance with the truth."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "You have come from afar, Sabhiya," said the Buddha, "wishing to ask some questions. I shall solve them for you, answering your questions in turn, in accordance with the truth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Ask me your question, Sabhiya, whatever you want. I'll solve each and every question you have."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Sabhiya thought, "Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing! Where those other ascetics and brahmins didn't even give me a chance, the Buddha has invited me." Uplifted and elated, full of rapture and happiness, he asked this question.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "What must one attain to be called a mendicant?" said Sabhiya, "How is one 'gentle', how said to be 'tamed'? How is one declared to be 'awakened'? May the Buddha please answer my question."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "When by the path they have walked themselves," said the Buddha to Sabhiya, "they reach extinguishment, with doubt overcome; giving up desire for existence or nonexistence, their journey complete, their rebirths ended: that is a mendicant.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Equanimous toward everything, mindful, they don't harm anyone in the world. An ascetic who has crossed over, unclouded, who has no pretensions, is gentle.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Their faculties have been developed inside and out in the whole world. Having pierced through this world and the next, tamed, they await their time.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have examined the eons in their entirety, and both sides of transmigration—passing away and rebirth. Rid of dust, unblemished, purified: the one they call 'awakened' has attained the end of rebirth."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And then, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, uplifted and elated, full of rapture and happiness, Sabhiya asked another question:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "What must one attain to be called 'brahmin'?" said Sabhiya. "Why is one an 'ascetic', and how a 'bathed initiate'? How is one declared to be a 'giant'? May the Buddha please answer my question."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Having banished all bad things," said the Buddha to Sabhiya, "immaculate, well-composed, steadfast, consummate, they've left transmigration behind: unattached, one such is called 'brahmin'.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: An assuaged one who has given up good and evil, stainless, understanding this world and the next, gone beyond rebirth and death: one such is rightly called 'ascetic'.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having washed off all bad things inside and out in the whole world, among gods and humans bound to creations, the one they call 'washed' does not return to creation.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They do nothing monstrous at all in the world, discarding all yokes and bonds, everywhere not stuck, freed: one such is rightly called 'giant'."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And then Sabhiya asked another question:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Who is a 'field-victor' according to the Buddhas?" said Sabhiya, "Why is one 'skillful', and how 'an astute scholar'? How is one declared to be a 'sage'? May the Buddha please answer my question."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "They are victors on the fields of deeds in their entirety," said the Buddha to Sabhiya, "the fields of gods, humans, and divinities; released from the root bondage to all fields: one such is rightly called 'field-victor'.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have examined the coffers in their entirety, the coffers of gods, humans, and divinities; released from the root bondage to all coffers: one such is rightly called 'skillful'.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have examined whiteness both inside and out; understanding purity, they have left dark and bright behind: one such is rightly called 'an astute scholar'.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Understanding the nature of the bad and the good inside and out in the whole world; one worthy of honor by gods and humans, who has escaped from the net and the chain: that is a sage."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And then Sabhiya asked another question:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "What must one attain to be called 'knowledge master'?" said Sabhiya, "Why is one 'studied', and how is one 'heroic'? How to gain the name 'thoroughbred'? May the Buddha please answer my question."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "They have examined knowledges in their entirety," said the Buddha to Sabhiya, "those that are current among ascetics and brahmins; rid of greed for all feelings, having left all knowledges behind: that is a knowledge master.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having studied proliferation and name & form inside and out—the root of disease; released from the root bondage to all disease: one such is rightly called 'studied'.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Refraining from all evil here, heroic, he escapes from the suffering of hell; he is heroic and energetic: one such is rightly called 'hero'.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Whoever's bonds are cut, the root of clinging inside and out; released from the root bondage to all clinging: one such is rightly called 'thoroughbred'."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And then Sabhiya asked another question:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "What must one attain to be called 'scholar'?" said Sabhiya, "Why is one 'noble', and how is one 'well conducted'? How to gain the name 'wanderer'? May the Buddha please answer my question."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "One who has learned every teaching," said the Buddha to Sabhiya, "and has known for themselves what in the world is blameworthy and blameless; a vanquisher, decided, liberated, untroubled everywhere: they call them 'scholar'.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having cut off defilements and clingings, being wise, they enter no womb. They've cast aside the bog of the three perceptions, the one they call 'noble' does not return to creation.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One here who is accomplished and skillful in all forms of good conduct; always understanding the teaching, everywhere not stuck, freed in mind, who has no aversion: they are 'well-conducted'.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They wander full of wisdom, having banished any deed that results in suffering, deceit and conceit, as well as greed and anger, above, below, all round, between. They have made a limit on name and form; the one they call a 'wanderer' has reached their destination."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And then, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, uplifted and elated, full of rapture and happiness, Sabhiya rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and extolled the Buddha in his presence with fitting verses:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "O one of vast wisdom, there are three and sixty opinions based on the doctrines of ascetics: they are expressions of perception, based on perception. Having dispelled them all, you passed over the dark flood.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You have gone to the end, gone beyond suffering, you are perfected, a fully awakened Buddha; I think you have ended defilements. Brilliant, thoughtful, abounding in wisdom, ender of suffering—you brought me across!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When you understood my uncertainty, you brought me beyond doubt—homage to you! A sage, accomplished in the ways of sagacity, you are gentle, not hardhearted, O Kinsman of the Sun.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Any doubts that I once had, you have answered for me, O Clear-eyed One. Clearly you are a sage, an Awakened One, there are no hindrances in you.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: All your distress is blown away and mown down. Cooled, tamed, steadfast: truth is your strength.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: O giant among giants, O great hero, when you are speaking all the gods rejoice, including both Nārada and Pabbata.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Homage to you, O thoroughbred! Homage to you, supreme among men! In the world with its gods, you have no rival.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You are the Buddha, you are the Teacher, you are the sage who has overcome Māra; you have cut off the underlying tendencies, you've crossed over, and you bring humanity across.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You have transcended attachments, your defilements are shattered; you are a lion free of grasping, with fear and dread given up.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Like a graceful lotus to which water does not stick, so both good and evil do not stick to you. Stretch out your feet, great hero: Sabhiya bows to the Teacher."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then the wanderer Sabhiya bowed with his head to the Buddha's feet and said, "Excellent, sir! Excellent! … I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha. Sir, may I receive the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha's presence?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Sabhiya, if someone formerly ordained in another sect wishes to take the going forth, the ordination in this teaching and training, they must spend four months on probation. When four months have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, they'll give the going forth, the ordination into monkhood. However, I recognize individual differences in this matter."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Sir, if four months probation are required in such a case, I'll spend four years on probation. When four years have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, let them give me the going forth, the ordination into monkhood." And the wanderer Sabhiya received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha's presence. And Venerable Sabhiya became one of the perfected.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering together with a large Saṅgha of 1,250 mendicants in the land of the Aṅguttarāpans when he arrived at a town of theirs named Āpaṇa. The matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya heard: "It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Āpaṇa, together with a large Saṅgha of 1,250 mendicants. He has this good reputation: 'That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.' He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others. He teaches Dhamma that's good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that's entirely full and pure. It's good to see such perfected ones."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So Keṇiya approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired him with a Dhamma talk. Then he said to the Buddha, "Would Worthy Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha please accept tomorrow's meal from me?" When he said this, the Buddha said to him, "The Saṅgha is large, Keṇiya; there are 1,250 mendicants. And you are devoted to the brahmins."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For a second time, Keṇiya asked the Buddha to accept a meal offering. "Never mind that the Saṅgha is large, with 1,250 mendicants, and that I am devoted to the brahmins. Would Worthy Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha please accept tomorrow's meal from me?" And for a second time, the Buddha gave the same reply.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For a third time, Keṇiya asked the Buddha to accept a meal offering. "Never mind that the Saṅgha is large, with 1,250 mendicants, and that I am devoted to the brahmins. Would Worthy Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha please accept tomorrow's meal from me?" The Buddha consented with silence. Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, Keṇiya rose from his seat and went to his own hermitage. There he addressed his friends and colleagues, relatives and kin, "My friends and colleagues, relatives and kin: please listen! The ascetic Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha has been invited by me for tomorrow's meal. Please help me out with the manual preparations." "Yes, worthy sir," they replied. Some dug ovens, some chopped wood, some washed dishes, some set up a water jar, and some spread out seats. Meanwhile, Keṇiya set up the pavilion himself.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Now at that time the brahmin Sela was residing in Āpaṇa. He had mastered the three Vedas, together with their vocabularies and ritual performance, their phonology and word classification, and the testaments as fifth. He knew them word-by-word, and their grammar. He was well versed in cosmology and the marks of a great man. And he was teaching three hundred young students to recite the hymns.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And at that time Keṇiya was devoted to Sela. Then Sela, while going for a walk escorted by the three hundred young students, approached Keṇiya's hermitage. He saw the preparations going on, and said to Keṇiya, "Worthy Keṇiya, is your son or daughter being married? Or are you setting up a grand sacrifice? Or has King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha been invited for tomorrow's meal?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "There is no marriage, Worthy Sela, and the king is not coming. Rather, I am setting up a grand sacrifice. The ascetic Gotama has arrived at Āpaṇa, together with a large Saṅgha of 1,250 mendicants. He has this good reputation: 'That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.' He has been invited by me for tomorrow's meal together with the mendicant Saṅgha." "Did you say 'the awakened one'?" "I said 'the awakened one'." "Did you say 'the awakened one'?" "I said 'the awakened one'."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Sela thought: "It's hard to even find the word 'awakened one' in the world. The thirty-two marks of a great man have been handed down in our hymns. A great man who possesses these has only two possible destinies, no other. If he stays at home he becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch, a just and principled king. His dominion extends to all four sides, he achieves stability in the country, and he possesses the seven treasures. He has the following seven treasures: the wheel, the elephant, the horse, the jewel, the woman, the householder, and the commander as the seventh treasure. He has over a thousand sons who are valiant and heroic, crushing the armies of his enemies. After conquering this land girt by sea, he reigns by principle, without rod or sword. But if he goes forth from the lay life to homelessness, he becomes a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha, who has cast off the world's veil." He said, "But Keṇiya, where is the Blessed One at present, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When he said this, Keṇiya pointed with his right arm and said, "There, worthy Sela, at that line of blue forest." Then Sela, together with his young students, approached the Buddha. He said to his young students, "Come quietly, gentlemen, tread gently. For the Buddhas are intimidating, like a lion living alone. When I'm consulting with the ascetic Gotama, don't interrupt. Wait until I've finished speaking."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Sela went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side, and scrutinized the Buddha's body for the thirty-two marks of a great man. He saw all of them except two, which he had doubts about: whether the private parts were sheathed in a foreskin, and the largeness of the tongue.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then it occurred to the Buddha, "Sela sees all the marks except two, which he has doubts about: whether the private parts are sheathed in a foreskin, and the largeness of the tongue." The Buddha used his psychic power to will that Sela would see his private parts sheathed in a foreskin. And he stuck out his tongue and stroked back and forth on his ear holes and nostrils, and covered his entire forehead with his tongue.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Sela thought, "The ascetic Gotama possesses the thirty-two marks completely, lacking none. But I don't know whether or not he is an awakened one. I have heard that brahmins of the past who were elderly and senior, the tutors of tutors, said, 'Those who are perfected ones, fully awakened Buddhas reveal themselves when praised.' Why don't I extoll him in his presence with fitting verses?" Then Sela extolled the Buddha in his presence with fitting verses:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "O Blessed One, your body's perfect, you're radiant, handsome, lovely to behold; golden colored, with teeth so white; you're strong.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The characteristics of a handsome man, the marks of a great man, are all found on your body.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Your eyes are clear, your face is fair, you're formidable, upright, majestic. In the midst of the Saṅgha of ascetics, you dazzle like the sun.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You're a mendicant fine to see, with skin that shines like lustrous gold. But with such excellent appearance, what do you want with the ascetic life?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You're fit to be a king, a wheel-turning monarch, chief of charioteers, victorious in the four quarters, lord of the Black Plum Tree Land.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Aristocrats, nobles, and kings ought follow your rule. Gotama, may you reign as king of kings, lord of mankind!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I am a king, Sela", said the Buddha, "the supreme king of the teaching. By the teaching I roll forth the wheel which cannot be rolled back."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "You claim to be awakened," said Sela the brahmin, "the supreme king of the teaching. 'I roll forth the teaching': so you say, Gotama.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then who is your general, the disciple who follows the Teacher's way? Who keeps rolling the wheel of the teaching you rolled forth?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "By me the wheel was rolled forth," said the Buddha, "the supreme wheel of the teaching. Sāriputta, taking after the Realized One, keeps it rolling on.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: I have known what should be known, and developed what should be developed, and given up what should be given up: and so, brahmin, I am a Buddha.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Dispel your doubt in me— make up your mind, brahmin! The sight of a Buddha is hard to find again.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: I am a Buddha, brahmin, the supreme surgeon, one of those whose appearance in the world is hard to find again.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A manifestation of divinity, unequaled, crusher of Māra's army; having subdued all my opponents, I rejoice, fearing nothing from any quarter."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Pay heed, good fellows, to what is spoken by the Clear-eyed One. The surgeon, the great hero, roars like a lion in the jungle.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A manifestation of divinity, unequaled, crusher of Māra's army; who would not be inspired by him, even one born in a dark class?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those who wish may follow me; those who don't may go. Right here, I'll go forth in his presence, the one of such outstanding wisdom."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Sir, if you endorse the teaching of the Buddha, we'll also go forth in his presence, the one of such outstanding wisdom."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "These three hundred brahmins with cupped palms held up, ask: 'May we lead the spiritual life in your presence, Blessed One?'"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The spiritual life is well explained," said the Buddha, "apparent in the present life, immediately effective. Here the going forth isn't in vain for one who trains with diligence."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And the brahmin Sela together with his assembly received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha's presence. And when the night had passed Keṇiya had delicious fresh and cooked foods prepared in his own hermitage. Then he had the Buddha informed of the time, saying, "It's time, worthy Gotama, the meal is ready." Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Keṇiya's hermitage, where he sat down on the seat spread out together with the Saṅgha of mendicants.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Keṇiya served and satisfied the mendicant Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods. When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Keṇiya took a low seat and sat to one side. The Buddha expressed his appreciation with these verses:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The foremost of sacrifices is the offering to the sacred flame; the Sāvitrī is the foremost of prayer; of humans, the king is the foremost; the ocean's the foremost of rivers;

author: Gotama Buddha
text: the foremost of stars is the moon; the sun is the foremost of blazes; for those who sacrifice seeking merit, the Saṅgha is the foremost."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When the Buddha had expressed his appreciation to Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic with these verses, he rose from his seat and left. Then Venerable Sela and his assembly, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. They lived having achieved with their own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness. And Venerable Sela together with his assembly became perfected.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Sela with his assembly went to the Buddha. He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his joined palms toward the Buddha, and said:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "This is the eighth day since we went for refuge, O Clear-eyed One. In these seven days, Blessed One, we've become tamed in your teaching.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You are the Buddha, you are the Teacher, you are the sage who has overcome Māra; you have cut off the underlying tendencies, you've crossed over, and you bring humanity across.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You have transcended attachments, your defilements are shattered; you are a lion free of grasping, with fear and dread given up.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: These three hundred mendicants stand with cupped palms raised. Stretch out your feet, great hero: let these giants bow to the Teacher."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Unforeseen and unknown is the extent of this mortal life— hard and short and bound to pain.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: There is no way that those born will not die. On reaching old age death follows: such is the nature of living creatures.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As ripe fruit are always in danger of falling, so mortals once born are always in danger of death.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As clay pots made by a potter all end up being broken, so is the life of mortals.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Young and old, foolish and wise— all go under the sway of death; all are destined to die.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When those overcome by death leave this world for the next, a father cannot protect his son, nor relatives their kin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: See how, while relatives look on, wailing profusely, mortals are led away one by one, like a cow to the slaughter.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And so the world is stricken by old age and by death. That is why the attentive do not grieve, for they understand the way of the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For one whose path you do not know— not whence they came nor where they went— you lament in vain, seeing neither end.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If a bewildered person, lamenting and self-harming, could extract any good from that, then those who see clearly would do the same.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For not by weeping and wailing will you find peace of heart. It just gives rise to more suffering, and distresses your body.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Growing thin and pale, you hurt yourself. It does nothing to help the dead: your lamentation is in vain.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Unless a personage gives up grief, they fall into suffering all the more. Bewailing those whose time has come, you fall under the sway of grief.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: See, too, other folk departing, passing on according to their deeds; fallen under the sway of death, beings flounder while still here.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For however they imagine it, it turns out to be something else. Such is separation: see the way of the world!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Even if a human lives a hundred years or more, they are parted from their family circle, they leave this life behind.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Therefore, having learned from the Perfected One, dispel lamentation. Seeing the dead and departed, think: "I cannot escape this."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As one would extinguish a blazing refuge with water, so too an attentive one—a wise, astute, and skilled person— would swiftly blow away grief that comes up, like the wind a tuft of cotton.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One who seeks their own happiness would pluck out the dart from themselves— the wailing and praying, and sadness inside.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: With dart plucked out, unattached, having found peace of mind, overcoming all sorrow, one is sorrowless and quenched.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala. Now at that time several very well-known well-to-do brahmins were residing in Icchānaṅgala. They included the brahmins Caṅkī, Tārukkha, Pokkharasāti, Jānussoṇi, Todeyya, and others. Then as the students Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja were going for a walk they began to discuss the question: "How do you become a brahmin?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Bhāradvāja said this: "When you're well born on both your mother's and father's side, stemming from a clean vessel, with irrefutable and impeccable genealogy back to the seventh paternal generation— then you're a brahmin."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Vāseṭṭha said this: "When you're ethical and accomplished in doing your duties— then you're a brahmin." But neither was able to persuade the other.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So Vāseṭṭha said to Bhāradvāja, "Worthy Bhāradvāja, the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—is staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala. He has this good reputation: 'That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.' Come, let's go to see him and ask him about this matter. As he answers, so we'll remember it." "Yes, worthy sir," replied Bhāradvāja.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So they went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side, and Vāseṭṭha addressed the Buddha in verse:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "We're both authorized masters of the three Vedas. I'm a student of Pokkharasāti, and he of Tārukkha.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: We're fully qualified in all the Vedic experts teach. As philologists and grammarians, we match our tutors in recitation.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: We have a dispute regarding genealogy. For Bhāradvāja says that one is a brahmin due to birth, but I declare it's because of one's deeds. Oh Clear-eyed One, know this as our debate.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Since neither of us was able to convince the other, we've come to ask you, sir, renowned as the awakened one.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As people honor with cupped palms the moon on the cusp of waxing, bowing, they revere Gotama in the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: We ask this of Gotama, the Eye arisen in the world: is one a brahmin due to birth, or else because of deeds? We don't know, please tell us, so we can recognize a brahmin."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I shall explain to you," said the Buddha, "accurately and in sequence, the taxonomy of living creatures, for species are indeed diverse.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Know the grass and trees, though they lack self-awareness. They're defined by birth, for species are indeed diverse.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Next there are bugs that crawl or fly, and so on, to ants and termites. They're defined by birth, for species are indeed diverse.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Know the quadrupeds, too, both small and large. They're defined by birth, for species are indeed diverse.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Know, too, the long-backed snakes, crawling on their bellies. They're defined by birth, for species are indeed diverse.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Next know the fish, whose habitat is the water. They're defined by birth, for species are indeed diverse.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Next know the birds, winged chariots in flight. They're defined by birth, for species are indeed diverse.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: While the differences between these species are defined by birth, the differences between humans are not defined by birth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not by hair nor by head, not by ear nor by eye, not by mouth nor by nose, not by lips nor by eyebrow,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: not by shoulder nor by neck, not by belly nor by back, not by buttocks nor by breast, not by groin nor by genitals,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: not by hands nor by feet, not by fingers nor by nails, not by knees nor by thighs, not by color nor by voice: none of these are defined by birth as it is for other species.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: In specific human bodies you can't find such distinctions. The distinctions among humans are spoken of by convention.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Anyone among humans who lives off keeping cattle: know them, Vāseṭṭha, as a farmer, not a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Anyone among humans who lives off various professions: know them, Vāseṭṭha, as a professional, not a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Anyone among humans who lives off trade: know them, Vāseṭṭha, as a trader, not a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Anyone among humans who lives off serving others: know them, Vāseṭṭha, as a servant, not a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Anyone among humans who lives off stealing: know them, Vāseṭṭha, as a bandit, not a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Anyone among humans who lives off archery: know them, Vāseṭṭha, as a warrior, not a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Anyone among humans who lives off priesthood: know them, Vāseṭṭha, as a sacrificer, not a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Anyone among humans who taxes village and nation, know them, Vāseṭṭha, as a ruler, not a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: I don't call someone a brahmin after the mother's womb they're born from. If they still have attachments, they're just someone who says 'worthy'. Having nothing, taking nothing: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having cut off all fetters they have no anxiety; they've slipped their chains and are detached: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've cut the strap and harness, the halter and bridle too; with cross-bar lifted, they're awakened: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Abuse, killing, caging: they endure these without anger. Patience is their powerful army: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not irritable or pretentious, dutiful in precepts and observances, tamed, bearing their final body: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Like water from a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed off the point of a pin, sensual pleasures slip off them: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They understand for themselves the end of suffering in this life; with burden put down, detached: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Deep in wisdom, intelligent, expert in the path and what is not the path; arrived at the highest goal: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Mixing with neither householders nor the homeless; a migrant with no bastion, few in wishes: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've laid aside violence against creatures firm and frail; not killing or making others kill: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not fighting among those who fight, quenched among those who have taken up arms, not grasping among those who grasp: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've discarded greed and hate, along with conceit and contempt, like a mustard seed off the point of a pin: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The words they utter are polished, informative, and true, and don't offend anyone: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They don't steal anything in the world, long or short, tiny or huge, beautiful or ugly: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have no hope for this world or the next; with no need for hope, detached: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have no clinging, knowledge has freed them of indecision, they've arrived at the objective, freedom from death: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've escaped clinging to both good and bad deeds; sorrowless, stainless, pure: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Pure as the spotless moon, clear and unclouded, they've ended relish for rebirth: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've got past this grueling swamp of delusion, transmigration. Meditating in stillness, free of indecision, they have crossed over to the far shore. They're quenched by not grasping: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've given up sensual pleasures, and have gone forth from lay life; they've ended rebirth in the sensual realm: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've given up craving, and have gone forth from lay life; they've ended craving to be reborn: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They've thrown off the human yoke, and slipped out of the heavenly yoke; unyoked from all yokes: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Giving up desire and discontent, they're cooled and free of attachments; a hero, master of the whole world: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They know the passing away and rebirth of all beings; unattached, holy, awakened: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Gods, centaurs, and humans don't know their destiny; the perfected ones with defilements ended: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have nothing before or after, or even in between. Having nothing, taking nothing: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Captain of the herd, excellent hero, great seer and victor; unstirred, washed, awakened: that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They who know their past lives, see heaven and places of loss, and have attained the ending of rebirth, that's who I declare a brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For name and clan are formulated as mere convention in the world. Produced by mutual agreement, they're formulated in each case.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For a long time this misconception has prejudiced those who don't understand. Ignorant, they declare that one is a brahmin by birth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You're not a brahmin by birth, nor by birth a non-brahmin. You're a brahmin by your deeds, and by deeds a non-brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You're a farmer by your deeds, by deeds you're a professional; you're a trader by your deeds, by deeds are you a servant;

author: Gotama Buddha
text: you're a bandit by your deeds, by deeds you're a warrior; you're a sacrificer by your deeds, by deeds you're a ruler.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: In this way the astute regard deeds in accord with truth. Seeing dependent origination, they're expert in deeds and their results.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Deeds make the world go on, deeds make people go on; sentient beings are bound by deeds, like a moving chariot's linchpin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: By fervor and spiritual practice, by restraint and by self-control: that's how to become a brahmin, this is the supreme brahmin.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Accomplished in the three knowledges, peaceful, with rebirth ended, know them, Vāseṭṭha, as the Divinity and Sakka to the wise."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When he had spoken, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja said to him, "Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! … From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then the mendicant Kokālika went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him, "Sir, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have corrupt wishes. They've fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When this was said, the Buddha said to Kokālika, "Don't say that, Kokālika! Don't say that, Kokālika! Have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna, they're good monks."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For a second time … For a third time Kokālika said to the Buddha, "Despite my faith and trust in the Buddha, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have corrupt wishes. They've fallen under the sway of corrupt wishes." For a third time, the Buddha said to Kokālika, "Don't say that, Kokālika! Don't say that, Kokālika! Have confidence in Sāriputta and Moggallāna, they're good monks."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then Kokālika rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving. Not long after he left his body erupted with boils the size of mustard seeds. The boils grew to the size of mung beans, then chickpeas, then jujube seeds, then jujubes, then myrobalans, then unripe wood-apples, then ripe wood-apples. Finally they burst open, and pus and blood oozed out. Then the mendicant Kokālika died of that illness. He was reborn in the Pink Lotus hell because of his resentment for Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then, late at night, the glorious divinity Sahampati, lighting up the entire Jeta's Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and said to him, "Sir, the mendicant Kokālika has passed away. He was reborn in the Pink Lotus hell because of his resentment for Sāriputta and Moggallāna." That is what the divinity Sahampati said. Then he bowed and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before vanishing right there.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then, when the night had passed, the Buddha told the mendicants all that had happened.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha, "Sir, how long is the lifespan in the Pink Lotus hell?" "It's long, mendicant. It's not easy to calculate how many years, how many hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of years it lasts." "But sir, is it possible to give a simile?" "It's possible," said the Buddha.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Suppose there was a Kosalan load of twenty packs of sesame seed. And at the end of every hundred years someone would remove a single seed from it. By this means the Kosalan load of twenty packs of sesame seed would run out faster than a single lifetime in the Abbuda hell. Now, twenty lifetimes in the Abbuda hell equal one lifetime in the Nirabbuda hell. Twenty lifetimes in the Nirabbuda hell equal one lifetime in the Ababa hell. Twenty lifetimes in the Ababa hell equal one lifetime in the Aṭaṭa hell. Twenty lifetimes in the Aṭaṭa hell equal one lifetime in the Ahaha hell. Twenty lifetimes in the Ahaha hell equal one lifetime in the Yellow Lotus hell. Twenty lifetimes in the Yellow Lotus hell equal one lifetime in the Fragrant Water Lily hell. Twenty lifetimes in the Fragrant Water Lily hell equal one lifetime in the Blue Water Lily hell. Twenty lifetimes in the Blue Water Lily hell equal one lifetime in the White Lotus hell. Twenty lifetimes in the White Lotus hell equal one lifetime in the Pink Lotus hell. The mendicant Kokālika has been reborn in the Pink Lotus hell because of his resentment for Sāriputta and Moggallāna." That is what the Buddha said. Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "A person is born with an axe in their mouth. A fool cuts themselves with it when they say bad words.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When you praise someone worthy of criticism, or criticize someone worthy of praise, you choose a losing hand with your own mouth: you'll never find happiness that way.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A losing hand at dice is a trivial thing, if all you lose is your money and all you own, even yourself. What's a really terrible hand is to hate the holy ones.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For a hundred thousand times a hundred million, times five hundred and thirty-six times a thousand times ten million years a slanderer of noble ones goes to hell, having aimed bad words and thoughts at them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A liar goes to hell, as does one who denies what they did. Both are equal in the hereafter, those men of base deeds.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Whoever wrongs a man who has done no wrong, a pure man who has not a blemish, the evil backfires on the fool, like fine dust thrown upwind.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One addicted to the way of greed, abuses others with their speech, faithless, miserly, uncharitable, stingy, addicted to backbiting.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Foul-mouthed, divisive, ignoble, a baby-killer, wicked, wrongdoer, worst of men, cursed, base-born— quiet now, for you are bound for hell.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You stir up dust, causing harm, when you, sinner, malign the good. Having done many bad deeds, you'll go to the pit for a long time.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For no one's deeds are ever lost, they return to their owner. In the next life that stupid sinner sees suffering in themselves.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They approach the place of impalement, with its iron spikes, sharp blades, and iron stakes. Then there is the food, which appropriately, is like a red-hot iron ball.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For the speakers speak not sweetly, they don't hurry there, or find shelter. They lie upon a spread of coals, they enter a blazing mass of fire.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Wrapping them in a net, they strike them there with iron hammers. They come to blinding darkness, which spreads about them like a fog.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Next they enter a copper pot, a blazing mass of fire. There they roast for a long time, writhing in the masses of fire.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then the sinner roasts there in a mixture of pus and blood. No matter where they settle, everything they touch there hurts them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The sinner roasts in worm-infested water. There's not even a shore to go to, for all around are the same kind of pots.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They enter the Sword-Leaf Forest, so sharp they cut their body to pieces. Having grabbed the tongue with a hook, they stab it, slashing back and forth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then they approach the impassable Vetaraṇī River, with its sharp blades, its razor blades. Dullards fall into it, the wicked who have done wicked deeds.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: There dogs all brown and spotted, and raven flocks, and greedy jackals devour them as they wail, while hawks and crows attack them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Hard, alas, is the life here that sinners endure. That's why for the rest of this life a person ought do their duty without fail.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Experts have counted the loads of sesame as compared to the Pink Lotus hell. For there are five times ten thousand times ten million, plus another twelve hundred times ten million years—

author: Gotama Buddha
text: as painful as life is said to be in hell, that's how long one must dwell there. That's why, for those who are pure, well-behaved, full of good qualities, one should always guard one's speech and mind."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The seer Asita in his daily meditation saw the bright-clad gods of the host of Thirty and their lord Sakka joyfully celebrating, waving streamers in exuberant exaltation.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Seeing the gods rejoicing, elated, he paid respects and said this there: "Why is the community of gods in such excellent spirits? Why take up streamers and whirl them about?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Even in the war with the titans, when gods were victorious and titans defeated, there was no such excitement. What marvel have the celestials seen that they so rejoice?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Shouting and singing and playing music, they clap their hands and dance. I ask you, dwellers on Mount Meru's peak, quickly dispel my doubt, good fellows!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The being intent on awakening, a peerless gem, has been born in the human realm for the sake of welfare and happiness, in Lumbinī, a village in the Sakyan land. That's why we're so happy, in such excellent spirits.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He is supreme among all beings, the peak individual, captain of men, supreme among all creatures. He will roll forth the wheel in the grove of the seers, roaring like a mighty lion, lord of beasts."

author: Gotama Buddha
