text: Hearing this, he swiftly descended and right away approached Suddhodana's home. Seated there he said this to the Sakyans, "Where is the boy? I too wish to see him!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then the Sakyans showed their son to the one named Asita— the boy shone like burning gold well-wrought in the forge; dazzling with glory, of peerless beauty.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The boy beamed like crested flame, pure as the moon, lord of stars traversing the sky, blazing like the sun free of stormclouds after the rains; seeing him, he was joyful, brimming with happiness.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The celestials held up a parasol in the sky, many-ribbed and thousand-circled; and golden-handled chowries waved— but none could see who held the chowries or the parasols.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When the matted hair seer named "Dark Splendor" had seen the boy like a gold ingot on a cream rug with a white parasol held over his head, he received him, elated and happy.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having received the Sakyan bull, the seeker, master of marks and hymns, lifted up his voice with confident heart: "He is supreme, the best of men!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But then, remembering he would depart this world, his spirits fell and his tears flowed. Seeing the weeping seer, the Sakyans said, "Surely there will be no threat to the boy?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Seeing the crestfallen Sakyans, the seer said, "I do not forsee harm befall the boy, and there will be no threat to him, not in the least; set your minds at ease.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: This boy shall reach the highest awakening. As one of perfectly purified vision, compassionate for the welfare of the many, he shall roll forth the wheel of the teaching; his spiritual path will become widespread.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But I have not long left in this life, I shall die before then. I will never hear the teaching of the one who bore the unequaled burden. That's why I'm so upset and distraught—it's a disaster for me!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having brought abundant happiness to the Sakyans, the spiritual seeker left the royal compound. He had a nephew; and out of sympathy he encouraged him in the teaching of the one who bore the unequaled burden.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "When you hear the voice of another saying 'Buddha'— one who has attained awakening and who reveals the foremost teaching— go there and ask about his breakthrough; lead the spiritual life under that Blessed One."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Now, that Nālaka had a store of accumulated merit; so when instructed by one of such kindly intent, with perfectly purified vision of the future, he waited anticipating the Victor, guarding his senses.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When he heard of the Victor rolling forth the excellent wheel he went to him, and seeing the boss seer, he became confident. The time of Asita's instruction had arrived; so he asked the excellent sage about the highest sagacity. The introductory verses are finished.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I now know that Asita's words have turned out to be true. I ask you this, Gotama, who has gone beyond all things:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For one who has entered the homeless life, seeking food on alms round, when questioned, O sage, please tell me of sagacity, the ultimate state."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I shall school you in sagacity," said the Buddha, "so difficult and challenging. Come, I shall tell you all about it. Brace yourself; stay strong!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: In the village, keep the same attitude no matter if reviled or praised. Guard against ill-tempered thoughts; wander peaceful and humble.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Many different things come up, like tongues of fire in a forest. Women try to seduce a sage— let them not seduce you!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Refraining from sex, having left behind sensual pleasures high and low, don't be hostile or attached to living creatures firm or frail.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'As am I, so are they; as are they, so am I'— Treating others like oneself, neither kill nor incite to kill.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Leaving behind desire and greed for what ordinary people are attached to, one whose eye is clear would set out to practice, they'd cross over this abyss.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: With empty stomach, taking limited food, few in wishes, not greedy; truly hungerless regarding all desires, desireless, one is quenched.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having wandered for alms, they'd take themselves into the forest; and nearing the foot of a tree, the sage would take their seat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That attentive one intent on absorption, would delight within the forest. They'd practice absorption at the foot of a tree, filling themselves with bliss.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then, at the end of the night, they'd take themselves into a village. They'd not welcome being called, nor offerings brought from the village.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A sage who has come to a village would not walk hastily among the families. They'd not discuss their search for food, nor would they speak suggestively.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'I got something, that's good. I got nothing, that's fine.' Unaffected in both cases, they return right to the tree.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Wandering with bowl in hand, not dumb, but thought to be dumb, they wouldn't scorn a tiny gift, nor look down upon the giver.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For the practice has many aspects, as revealed by the Ascetic. They do not go to the far shore twice, nor having gone once do they fall away.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When a mendicant has no creeping, and has cut the stream of craving, and given up all the various duties, no fever is found in them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: I shall school you in sagacity. Practice as if you were licking a razor's edge. With tongue pressed against the roof of your mouth, be restrained regarding your stomach.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Don't be sluggish in mind, nor think overly much. Be free of putrefaction and unattached, committed to the spiritual life.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Train in a lonely seat, attending closely to ascetics; solitude is sagacity, they say. If you welcome solitude, you'll light up the ten directions.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having heard the words of the attentive, the meditators who've given up sensual desires, a follower of mine would develop conscience and faith all the more.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Understand this by the way streams move in clefts and crevices: the little creeks flow on resounding, while silent flow the great rivers.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: What is lacking, resounds; what is full is at peace. The fool is like a half-full pot; the wise like a brimfull lake.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When the Ascetic speaks much it is relevant and meaningful: knowing, he teaches the Dhamma; knowing, he speaks much.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But one who, knowing, is self-controlled, knowing, does not speak much; that sage is worthy of sagacity, that sage has achieved sagacity."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the stilt longhouse of Migāra's mother in the Eastern Monastery. Now, at that time it was the sabbath—the full moon on the fifteenth day—and the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks. Then the Buddha looked around the Saṅgha of monks, who were so very silent. He addressed them:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Suppose, monks, they questioned you thus: 'There are skillful teachings that are noble, emancipating, and lead to awakening. What is the real reason for listening to such teachings?' You should answer: 'Only so as to truly know the pairs of teachings.' And what pairs do they speak of?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering': this is the first contemplation. 'This is the cessation of suffering; this is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates rightly contemplating a pair of teachings in this way—diligent, keen, and resolute—they can expect one of two results: enlightenment in this very life, or if there's residue left behind, non-return."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That is what the Buddha said. Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "There are those who don't understand suffering and suffering's cause, and where all suffering ceases no residue left behind. And they do not know the path that leads to the stilling of suffering.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They lack the heart's release, as well as the release by wisdom. Unable to make an end, they continue to be reborn and grow old.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But there are those who understand suffering and suffering's cause, and where all suffering ceases with no residue left behind. And they understand the path that leads to the stilling of suffering.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They're endowed with the heart's release, as well as the release by wisdom. Able to make an end, they don't continue to be reborn and grow old."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Suppose, monks, they questioned you thus: 'Could there be another way to contemplate the pairs?' You should say, 'There could.' And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by attachment': this is one contemplation. 'When attachment has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Attachment is the source of suffering in all its countless forms in the world. When an ignorant person builds up attachments, that dullard returns to suffering again and again. So let one who understands not build up attachments, contemplating the inception of suffering and rebirth."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Suppose, monks, they questioned you thus: 'Could there be another way to contemplate the pairs?' You should say, 'There could.' And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by ignorance': this is one contemplation. 'When ignorance has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Those who journey again and again, transmigrating through birth and death; they go from this state to another, that destination due only to ignorance.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For ignorance is the great delusion because of which we have long transmigrated. Those beings who have knowledge do not proceed to a future life."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by choices': this is one contemplation. 'When choices has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "All the suffering that originates is caused by choices. With the cessation of choices, there is no origination of suffering.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing this danger, that suffering is caused by choices; through the stilling of all choices, and the stopping of perceptions, this is the way suffering ends when one has known this as it is.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Rightly seeing, knowledge masters, the astute, understanding rightly, having thrown off Māra's yoke, do not proceed to a future life."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by consciousness': this is one contemplation. 'When consciousness has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "All the suffering that originates is caused by consciousness. With the cessation of consciousness, there is no origination of suffering.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing this danger, that suffering is caused by consciousness, with the stilling of consciousness a mendicant is hungerless, quenched."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by contact': this is one contemplation. 'When contact has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Those mired in contact, swept down the stream of lives, practicing the wrong way, are far from the ending of fetters.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But those who completely understand contact, who, understanding, delight in peace; by comprehending contact they are hungerless, quenched."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by feeling': this is one contemplation. 'When feeling has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Whether it's pleasant or painful, as well as what's neutral, whatever there is that is felt internally and externally:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: having known, 'this is suffering, deceptive, breaking apart', seeing feelings vanish with every contact, that's how they understand them. With the ending of feelings, a mendicant is hungerless, quenched."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by craving': this is one contemplation. 'When craving has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Craving is a person's partner as they transmigrate on this long journey. They go from this state to another, but don't escape transmigration.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing this danger, that craving is the cause of suffering— rid of craving, free of grasping, a mendicant would wander mindful."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by grasping': this is one contemplation. 'When grasping has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Grasping is the cause of continued existence; one who exists falls into suffering. Death comes to those who are born— this is the origination of suffering.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That's why with the end of grasping, the astute, understanding rightly, having directly known the end of rebirth, do not proceed to a future life."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by instigating activity': this is one contemplation. 'When instigation has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "All the suffering that originates is caused by instigating activity. With the cessation of instigation, there is no origination of suffering.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing this danger, that suffering is caused by instigating activity, having given up all instigation, one is freed with respects to instigation.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For the mendicant with peaceful mind, who has cut off craving for continued existence, transmigration through births is finished; there'll be no more future lives for them."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by sustenance': this is one contemplation. 'When sustenance has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "All the suffering that originates is caused by sustenance. With the cessation of sustenance, there is no origination of suffering.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing this danger, that suffering is caused by sustenance, completely understanding all sustenance, one is independent of all sustenance.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having rightly understood the state of health, through the ending of defilements, one who makes use after appraisal, firm in principle, a knowledge master cannot be reckoned."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'All the suffering that originates is caused by perturbation': this is one contemplation. 'When perturbation has faded away and ceased with no residue left behind, there is no origination of suffering': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "All the suffering that originates is caused by perturbation. With the cessation of perturbation, there is no origination of suffering.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing this danger, that suffering is caused by perturbation, that's why, having relinquished perturbation, and stopped making karmic choices, imperturbable, free of grasping, a mendicant would wander mindful."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'For the dependent there is quivering': this is the first contemplation. 'For the independent there's no agitation': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "For the independent there's no agitation. The dependent, grasping, goes from this state to another, without escaping transmigration.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing this danger, the great fear in dependencies, independent, free of grasping, a mendicant would wander mindful."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'Formless states are more peaceful than states of form': this is the first contemplation. 'Cessation is more peaceful than formless states': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "There are beings in the realm of luminous form, and others stuck in the formless. Not understanding cessation, they return in future lives.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But the people who completely understand form, not stuck in the formless, released in cessation— they are conquerors of death."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "'Could there be another way?' … And how could there be? 'What this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—focuses on as true, the noble ones have clearly seen with right wisdom to be actually false': this is the first contemplation. 'What this world focuses on as false, the noble ones have clearly seen with right wisdom to be actually true': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates in this way they can expect enlightenment or non-return." Then the Teacher went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "See how the world with its gods imagines not-self to be self; habituated to name and form, imagining this is truth.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For however they imagine it, it turns out to be something else. And that is what is false in it, for the ephemeral is deceptive by nature.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Extinguishment has an undeceptive nature, the noble ones know it as truth. Having comprehended the truth, they are hungerless, quenched."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Suppose, monks, they questioned you thus: 'Could there be another way to contemplate the pairs?' You should say, 'There could.' And how could there be? 'What this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—focuses on as happiness, the noble ones have clearly seen with right wisdom to be actually suffering': this is the first contemplation. 'What this world focuses on as suffering, the noble ones have clearly seen with right wisdom to be actually happiness': this is the second contemplation. When a mendicant meditates rightly contemplating a pair of teachings in this way—diligent, keen, and resolute—they can expect one of two results: enlightenment in this very life, or if there's residue left behind, non-return." That is what the Buddha said. Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Sights, sounds, tastes, smells, touches, and ideas, the lot of them— they're likable, desirable, and pleasurable as long as you can say that they exist.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For all the world with its gods, this is what they deem happiness. And where they cease is deemed as suffering for them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The noble ones have seen as happiness the ceasing of substantial reality. This insight by those who see contradicts the whole world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: What others say is happiness the noble ones say is suffering. What others say is suffering the noble ones know as happiness.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: See, this teaching is hard to understand, it confuses the ignorant. There is darkness for the shrouded; blackness for those who don't see.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But the good are open; like light for those who see. Though close, they do not understand, those fools inexpert in the teaching.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They're mired in desire for continued existence, flowing along the stream of lives, mired in Māra's dominion: this teaching isn't easy for them to understand.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Who, apart from the noble ones, is qualified to understand this state? Having rightly understood this state, the undefiled are fully extinguished."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That is what the Buddha said. Satisfied, the monks approved what the Buddha said. And while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of sixty monks were freed from defilements by not grasping.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If a mortal desires sensual pleasure and their desire succeeds, they definitely become elated, having got what they want.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But for that personage in the throes of pleasure, aroused by desire, when those pleasures fade, it inflicts them like an arrow strike.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One who, being mindful, avoids sensual pleasures like side-stepping a snake's head, transcends attachment to the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: There are many objects of sensual desire: fields, lands, and gold; cattle and horses; slaves and servants; women and relatives. When a man lusts over these,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: the weak overpower him and adversities crush him. Suffering follows him like water in a leaky boat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That's why a personage, ever mindful, should avoid sensual pleasures. Give them up and cross the flood, as a bailed-out boat reaches the far shore.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Trapped in a cave, thickly overspread, sunk in delusion they stay. That sort is far from seclusion, for sensual pleasures in the world are not easy to give up.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The chains of desire, the bonds of life's pleasures are hard to escape, for one cannot free another. Looking to the past or the future, they pray for these pleasures or former ones.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Greedy, fixated, infatuated by sensual pleasures, they are incorrigible, habitually immoral. When led to suffering they lament, "What will become of us when we pass away from here?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That's why a personage should train in this life: should you know that anything in the world is wrong, don't act wrongly on account of that; for the attentive say this life is short.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: I see the world's population floundering, given to craving for future lives. Base men wail in the jaws of death, not rid of craving for life after life.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: See them flounder over belongings, like fish in puddles of a dried-up stream. Seeing this, live unselfishly, forming no attachment to future lives.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Rid of desire for both ends, having completely understood contact, free of greed, doing nothing for which they'd blame themselves, the attentive don't cling to the seen and the heard.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having completely understood perception and having crossed the flood, the sage, not clinging to possessions, with dart plucked out, living diligently, does not hope for this world or the next.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Some speak with malicious intent, while others speak set on truth. When disputes come up a sage does not get involved, which is why they've no barrenness at all.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: How can you transcend your own view when you're led by preference, dogmatic in belief? Inventing your own undertakings, you'd speak according to your notion.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Some personages, unasked, tell others of their own precepts and vows. They have an ignoble nature, say those who are skilled, since they speak on themselves of their own accord.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A mendicant, peaceful, quenched, never boasts "thus am I" of their precepts. They have a noble nature, say those who are skilled, who have no pretensions about anything in the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For one who formulates and creates teachings, and promotes them despite their defects, if they see an advantage for themselves, they become dependent on that, relying on unstable peace.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: It's not easy to get over dogmatic views adopted after judging among the teachings. That's why, among all these dogmas, a person ditches one teaching and takes up another.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The cleansed one has no formulated view at all in the world about the different realms. Having given up illusion and conceit, by what path would they go? They are not involved.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For one who gets involved is embroiled in disputes about teachings— but how to dispute with the uninvolved? About what? For picking up and putting down is not what they do; they have shaken off all views in this very life.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I see someone pure, perfectly healthy; it is vision that grants a person purity." Recalling this notion of the ultimate, they believe in the notion that there is one who observes purity.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If a person were granted purity through what is seen, or if by a notion they could give up suffering, then one with attachments is purified by another: their view betrays them as one who asserts thus.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The brahmin speaks not of purity from another in terms of what has been seen, heard, or thought; or by precepts or vows. They are unsullied in the midst of good and evil, letting go what was picked up, without creating anything new here.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having let go the last they lay hold of the next; following impulse, they don't pass the chain. They grab on and let loose like a monkey grabbing and releasing a branch.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having undertaken their own vows, a personage visits various teachers, being attached to perception. One who knows, having comprehended the truth through the knowledges, does not visit various teachers, being of vast wisdom.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They are remote from all things seen, heard, or thought. Seeing them living openly, how could anyone in this world judge them?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They don't make things up or promote them, or speak of the uttermost purity. After untying the tight knot of grasping they long for nothing in the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The brahmin has stepped over the perimeter; knowing and seeing, they adopt nothing. Neither in love with passion nor besotted by dispassion, there is nothing here they adopt as the ultimate.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If, maintaining that theirs is the "ultimate" view, a personage makes it out to be highest in the world; then they declare all others are "lesser"; that's why they're not beyond disputes.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If they see an advantage for themselves in what's seen, heard, or thought; or in precepts or vows, in that case, having adopted that one alone, they see all others as inferior.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those who are skilled say that, too, is a knot, relying on which people see others as lesser. That's why a mendicant ought not rely on what's seen, heard, or thought, or on precepts and vows.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Nor would they form a view about the world through a notion or through precepts and vows. They would never represent themselves as "equal", nor conceive themselves "worse" or "better".

author: Gotama Buddha
text: What was picked up has been set down and is not grasped again; they form no dependency even on notions. They follow no side among the factions, and believe in no view at all.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One here who has no wish for either end— for any state of existence in this life or the next— has adopted no dogma at all after judging among the teachings.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For them not even the tiniest idea is formulated here regarding what is seen, heard, or thought. That brahmin does not grasp any view— how could anyone in this world judge them?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They don't make things up or promote them, and don't subscribe to any of the doctrines. The brahmin has no need to be led by precept or vow; gone to the far shore, one such does not return.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Short, alas, is this life; you die before a hundred years. Even if you live a little longer, you still die of old age.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: People grieve over belongings, yet there is no such thing as permanent possessions. Separation is a fact of life; when you see this, you wouldn't stay living at home.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Whatever a person thinks of as belonging to them, that too is given up when they die. Knowing this, an astute follower of mine would not be bent on ownership.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Just as, upon awakening, a person does not see what they encountered in a dream; so too you do not see your loved ones when they are dead and gone.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: You used to see and hear those folk, and call them by their name. Yet the name is all that's left to tell of a personage when they're gone.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Those who are greedy for belongings don't give up sorrow, lamentation, and stinginess. That's why the sages, seers of sanctuary, left possessions behind and wandered.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For a mendicant who lives withdrawn, frequenting a secluded seat, they say it's fitting to not show themselves in a home.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The sage is independent everywhere, they don't form likes or dislikes. Lamentation and stinginess slip off them like water from a leaf.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Like a droplet slips from a lotus-leaf, like water from a lotus flower; the sage doesn't cling to that which is seen or heard or thought.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For the one who is cleansed does not conceive in terms of things seen, heard, or thought. They do not wish to be purified by another; they are neither passionate nor growing dispassioned.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "When someone indulges in sex," said Venerable Tissametteyya, "tell us, good fellow: what trouble befalls them? After hearing your instruction, we shall train in seclusion."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "When someone indulges in sex," replied the Buddha, "they forget their instructions and go the wrong way— that is something ignoble in them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Someone who formerly lived alone and then resorts to sex is like a chariot careening off-track; in the world they call them a low, ordinary person.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Their former fame and reputation also fall away. Seeing this, they'd train to give up sex.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Oppressed by thoughts, they brood like a wretch. When they hear what others are saying, that sort is embarrassed.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then they lash out with verbal daggers when reproached by others. This is their great blind spot; they sink to lies.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They once were considered astute, committed to the solitary life. But then they indulged in sex, dragged along by desire like a dullard.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing this danger in falling from a former state here, a sage would firmly resolve to wander alone, and would not resort to sex.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They'd train themselves only in seclusion; this, for the noble ones, is highest. One who'd not think themselves 'best' due to that has truly drawn near to extinguishment.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: People tied to sensual pleasures envy them: the isolated, wandering sage who has crossed the flood, unconcerned for sensual pleasures."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Here alone is purity," they say, denying that there is purification in other teachings. Speaking of the beauty in that which they depend on, each one is dogmatic about their own idiosyncratic interpretation.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Desiring debate, they plunge into an assembly, where each takes the other as a fool. Relying on others they state their contention, desiring praise while claiming to be skilled.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Addicted to debating in the midst of the assembly, their need for praise makes them nervous. But when they're repudiated they get embarrassed; upset at criticism, they find fault in others.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If their doctrine is said to be weak, and judges declare it repudiated, the loser weeps and wails, moaning, "They beat me."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When these disputes come up among ascetics, they get excited or dejected. Seeing this, refrain from contention, for the only purpose is praise and profit.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But if, having declared their doctrine, they are praised there in the midst of the assembly, they laugh and gloat because of it, having got what they wanted.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Their pride is their downfall, yet they speak from conceit and arrogance. Seeing this, one ought not dispute, for those who are skilled say this is no way to purity.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: As a warrior, after feasting on royal food, goes roaring, looking for someone to fight— go off and find an opponent, Sūra, for here, as before, there is no one to combat.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When someone disputes about a view they've adopted, saying, "This is the only truth," say to them, "Here you'll have no adversary when a dispute has come up."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: There are those who live far from the crowd, not countering views with view. Who is there to argue with you, Pasūra, among those who grasp nothing here as the highest?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And so you come along speculating, thinking up theories in your mind. Now that you've challenged someone who is cleansed, you'll not be able to respond.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Even when I saw the sirens Craving, Malignancy, and Lust, I had no desire for sex. What is this body full of piss and shit? I wouldn't even want to touch it with my foot."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "If you do not want a gem such as this, a lady desired by many lords of men, then what manner of theory, precepts and vows, livelihood, and rebirth in a new life do you assert?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "After judging among the teachings," said the Buddha to Māgaṇḍiya, "none have been adopted thinking, 'I assert this.' Seeing views without adopting any, searching, I saw inner peace."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "O sage, you speak of judgments you have formed," said Māgaṇḍiya, "without having adopted any of those views. As to that matter of 'inner peace'— how is that described by the attentive?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Purity is spoken of not as due to view," said the Buddha to Māgaṇḍiya, "learning, knowledge, or precepts and vows; nor without view, learning, knowledge, or precepts and vows. Having relinquished these, not adopting them, peaceful, independent, one would not pray for another life."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "It seems purity is spoken of not as due to view," said Māgaṇḍiya, "learning, knowledge, or precepts and vows; nor without view, learning, knowledge, or precepts and vows. If so, I think this teaching is sheer folly; some believe that purity comes from view."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Continuing to question while relying on a view," said the Buddha to Māgaṇḍiya, "you've become confused by all you've adopted. From this you've not glimpsed the slightest idea, which is why you consider the teaching folly.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If you think that 'I'm equal, special, or worse', you'll dispute about that. Not wavering due to the three discriminations, they have no thought, 'I'm equal or special'.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Why would that brahmin say, 'It's true', or with whom would they dispute, 'It's false'? There is no equal or unequal in them, so who would they take on in debate?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: After leaving their bastion to migrate without abode, a sage doesn't get close to anyone in town. Rid of sensual pleasures, not expecting, they wouldn't get in arguments with people.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A spiritual giant would not take up for debate the things in the world from which they live secluded. As a prickly lotus born in the water is unsullied by water and mud, so the greedless sage, proponent of peace, is unsmeared by sensuality and the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A knowledge master does not become conceited due to view or thought, for they are not determined by that. They've no need for deeds or learning, they're not indoctrinated in dogmas.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: There are no ties for one detached from ideas; there are no delusions for one freed by wisdom. But those who have adopted ideas and views wander the world causing conflict."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Seeing how, behaving how, is one said to be at peace? When asked, Gotama, please tell me about the ultimate person."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Rid of craving before the breakup," said the Buddha, "not dependent on the first beginning, unfathomable in the middle, they are not governed by anything.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Unangry, unafraid, not boastful or regretful, thoughtful in counsel, not restless— truly that sage is controlled in speech.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Rid of attachment to the future, they don't grieve for the past. A seer of seclusion in the midst of contacts is not led astray among views.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Withdrawn, free of deceit, they're not envious or stingy, nor rude or disgusting, or given to slander.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not swept up in pleasures, or given to arrogance, they're gentle and articulate, neither hungering nor growing dispassionate.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not training for desire for profit, nor getting annoyed at lack of profit; they are not hostile due to craving, for they are not greedy for flavors.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Equanimous, ever mindful, they never conceive themselves in the world as equal, special, or less than; they have no pretensions.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have no dependencies, understanding the teaching, they are independent. No craving is found in them to continue existence or to end it.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: I declare them to be at peace, unconcerned for sensual pleasures. No ties are found in them, they have crossed over clinging.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have no children or livestock, nor possess fields or lands. No picking up or putting down is found in them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That by which one might describe an ordinary person or ascetics and brahmins has no importance to them, which is why they're unperturbed by words.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Freed of greed, not stingy, a sage doesn't speak of themselves as being among superiors, inferiors, or equals. One not prone to creation does not return to creation.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They who have nothing in the world of their own do not grieve for that which is not, or drift among the teachings; that's who is said to be at peace."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Where do quarrels and disputes come from? And lamentation and sorrow, and stinginess? What of conceit and arrogance, and slander too— tell me please, where do they come from?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Quarrels and disputes come from what we hold dear, as do lamentation and sorrow, stinginess, conceit and arrogance. Quarrels and disputes are linked to stinginess, and when disputes have arisen there is slander."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "So where do things held dear in the world spring from? And the lusts that are loose in the world? Where spring the hopes and aims a man has for lives to come?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "What we hold dear in the world spring from desire, as do the lusts that are loose in the world. From there spring the hopes and aims a man has for lives to come."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "So where does desire in the world spring from? And evaluations, too, where do they come from? And anger, lies, and indecision, and other things spoken of by the Ascetic?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "What they call pleasure and pain in the world— based on that, desire comes about. Seeing the manifestation and vanishing of forms, a personage makes evaluations in the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Anger, lies, and indecision— these things are, too, when that pair is present. One who is indecisive should train in the path of knowledge; it is from knowledge that the Ascetic speaks of these things."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Where do pleasure and pain spring from? When what is absent do these things not occur? And also, on the topic of manifesting and vanishing— tell me where they spring from."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Pleasure and pain spring from contact; when contact is absent they do not occur. And on the topic of manifesting and vanishing— I tell you they spring from there."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "So where does contact in the world spring from? And possessions, too, where do they come from? When what is absent is there no possessiveness? When what vanishes do contacts not strike?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Name and form cause contact; possessions spring from wishing; when wishing is absent there is no possessiveness; when form vanishes, contacts don't strike."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Form vanishes for one proceeding how? And how do happiness and suffering vanish? Tell me how they vanish; I think we ought to know these things."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Without normal perception or distorted perception; not lacking perception, nor perceiving what has vanished. Form vanishes for one proceeding thus; for judgments due to proliferation spring from perception."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Whatever I asked you have explained to me. I ask you once more, please tell me this: Do some astute folk here say that this is the highest extent of purity of the spirit? Or do they say it is something else?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Some astute folk do say that this is the highest extent of purity of the spirit. But some of them, claiming to be experts, speak of an occasion when there is no residue.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Knowing that these states are dependent, and knowing what they depend on, the inquiring sage, having understood, is freed, and enters no dispute. The attentive do not proceed to life after life."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: "Each maintaining their own view, those who are skilled disagree, arguing: 'Whoever sees it this way understands the teaching; those who reject this are inadequate.'

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: So arguing, they dispute, saying, 'The other is a fool, an amateur!' Which of these is a true statement, for all of them profess to be experts?"

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: "If not accepting another's teaching makes you a useless fool lacking wisdom, then they're all fools lacking wisdom, for they all maintain their own view.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: But if having your own view makes you pristine— pure in wisdom, expert and thoughtful— then none of them lack wisdom, for such is the view they have all embraced.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: I do not say that it is correct when they call each other fools. Each has built up their own view to be the truth, which is why they take the other as a fool."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: "What some say is true and correct, others say is hollow and false. So arguing, they dispute; why don't ascetics say the same thing?"

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: "The truth is one, there is no second, understanding which folk would not dispute. But those ascetics each boast of different truths; that's why they don't say the same thing."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: "But why do they speak of different truths, these proponents who profess to be experts? Are there really so many different truths, or do they just follow their own lines of reasoning?"

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: "No, there are not many different truths that, apart from perception, are lasting in the world. Having formed their reasoning regarding different views, they say there are two things: true and false.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: The seen, heard, or thought, or precepts or vows— based on these they show disdain. Standing in judgment, they scoff, saying, 'The other is a fool, an amateur!'

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: They take the other as a fool on the same grounds that they speak of themselves as an expert. Professing to be expert on their own authority, they disdain the other while saying the same thing.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: They are perfect, according to their own extreme view; drunk on conceit, imagining themselves proficient. They have anointed themselves in their own mind, for such is the view they have embraced.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: If the word of your opponent makes you deficient, then they too are lacking wisdom. But if on your own authority you're a knowledge master, an attentive one, then there are no fools among the ascetics.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: 'Those who proclaim a teaching other than this have fallen short of purity, and are inadequate': so say each one of the sectarians, for they are deeply attached to their own view.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: 'Here alone is purity,' they say, denying that there is purification in other teachings. Thus each one of the sectarians, being dogmatic, speaks forcefully within the context of their own journey.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: But in that case, so long as they are speaking forcefully of their own journey, how can they take the other as a fool? They are the ones who provoke conflict when they call the other a fool with an impure teaching.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.12 The Shorter Discourse on Arrayed For Battle
text: Standing in judgment, measuring by their own standard, they dispute with the world more and more. But a personage who has given up all judgments creates no conflict in the world."

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: "Regarding those who maintain their own view, disputing that, 'This is the only truth': are all of them subject only to criticism, or do some also win praise for that?"

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: "That is a small thing, insufficient for peace, these two fruits of dispute, I say. Seeing this, one ought not dispute, looking for sanctuary in the land of no dispute.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: One who knows does not get involved with any of the many different conventions. Why would the uninvolved get involved, since they do not believe based on the seen or the heard?

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: Those for whom ethics are the highest speak of purity through self-control; having undertaken a vow, they stick to it: 'Let us train right here, then we will be pure.' Professing to be experts, they are led on to future lives.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: If they fall away from their precepts and vows, they tremble, having failed in their task. They pray and long for purity, like one who has lost their caravan while journeying far from home.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: But having given up all precepts and vows, and these deeds blameworthy or blameless; not longing for 'purity' or 'impurity', live detached, fostering peace.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: Relying on mortification in disgust of sin, or else on what is seen, heard, or thought, they moan that purification comes through heading upstream, not rid of craving for life after life.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: For one who longs there are muttered prayers, and trembling too over ideas they have formed. But one here for whom there is no passing away or reappearing: why would they tremble? For what would they pray?"

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: "The very same teaching that some say is 'ultimate', others say is inferior. Which of these statements is true, for all of them profess to be experts?"

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: "They say their own teaching is perfect, while the teaching of others is inferior. So arguing, they dispute, each saying their own conventions are the truth.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: If someone else's disparagement makes you inferior, no one in any teaching would be distinguished. For each of them says the other's teaching is lacking, while forcefully advocating their own.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: But if they honor their own teachings just as they praise their own journeys, then all doctrines would be equally valid, and purity would be specific to them.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: After judging among the teachings, a brahmin has adopted nothing that requires interpretation by another. That's why they've gotten over disputes, for they see no other doctrine as best.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: Saying, 'I know, I see, that's how it is', some believe that purity stems from view. But if they've really seen, what use is that view to them? Overlooking what matters, they say purity comes from another.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: When a person sees, they see name and form, and having seen, they will know just these things. Gladly let them see much or little, for those who are skilled say this is no way to purity.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: It's not easy to educate someone who is dogmatic, promoting a view they have formulated. Speaking of the beauty in that on which they depend, they talk of purity in accord with what they saw there.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: The brahmin does not get involved with formulating and calculating; they're not followers of views, nor kinsmen of notions. Having understood the many different conventions, they look on when others grasp.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: Having untied the knots here in the world, the sage takes no side among disputes. Peaceful among the peaceless, equanimous, they don't grasp when others grasp.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: Having given up former defilements and not making new ones, not swayed by preference, nor a proponent of dogma, that attentive one is released from views, not clinging to the world, nor reproaching themselves.

author: Gotama Buddha
division_title: 4.13 The Longer Discourse on Arrayed for Battle
text: They are remote from all things seen, heard, or thought. With burden put down, the sage is released: not formulating, not abstaining, not longing."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Great seer, I ask you, the Kinsman of the Sun, about seclusion and the state of peace. How, having seen, is a mendicant extinguished, not grasping anything in this world?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "They would cut off the idea, 'I am the thinker'," said the Buddha, "which is the root of all judgments that emerge from proliferation. Ever mindful, they would train to remove any internal cravings.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Regardless of what things they know, whether internal or external, they wouldn't be proud because of that, for that is not quenching, say the good.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They wouldn't let that make them conceited, thinking themselves better or worse or alike. When questioned in many ways, they wouldn't keep justifying themselves.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A mendicant would be settled internally, and not seek peace from another. For one at peace inside themselves, there's no picking up, whence putting down?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Just as, in the middle of the ocean, no waves arise, it stays still; so too one unstirred is still— a mendicant would make no pretension regarding anything."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "He whose eyes are open has explained the truth he witnessed, where adversities are removed. Please now speak of the practice, sir, the monastic code and immersion in samādhi."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "With eyes not wanton, they'd turn their ears from village gossip. They wouldn't be greedy for flavors, nor possessive about anything in the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Though struck by contacts, a mendicant would not lament at all. They wouldn't pray for another life, nor tremble in the face of dangers.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When they receive food and drink, edibles and clothes, they wouldn't store them up, nor worry about not getting them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Meditative, not footloose, they'd avoid remorse and not be negligent. Then a mendicant would stay in quiet places to sit and rest.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They wouldn't take much sleep, but, being keen, would apply themselves to wakefulness. They'd give up sloth, illusion, mirth, and play, and sex and ornamentation.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They wouldn't cast Artharvaṇa spells, interpret dreams or omens, or practice astrology. My followers would not study ominous animal cries, work as a doctor, or treat an impacted fetus.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not shaken by criticism, a mendicant would not gloat when praised. They'd cast aside greed and stinginess, anger, and slander.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They'd not stand for buying and selling; a mendicant would not speak ill at all. They wouldn't linger in the village, nor cajole people from desire for profit.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A mendicant would be no boaster, nor would they speak suggestively. They wouldn't train in impudence, nor speak argumentatively.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They wouldn't be led into lying, nor be deliberately devious. And they'd never look down on another because of livelihood, wisdom, or precepts and vows.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Though provoked from hearing much talk from ascetics saying all different things, they wouldn't react harshly, for the virtuous do not retaliate.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having understood this teaching, inquiring, a mendicant would always train mindfully. Knowing quenching as peace, they'd not be negligent in Gotama's bidding.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For he is the vanquisher, the unvanquished, seer of the truth as witness, not by legends— that's why, being diligent, they would always train respectfully in the Buddha's teaching."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Peril stems from those who take up arms— just look how people conflict! I shall extol how I came to be stirred with a sense of urgency.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: I saw this population flounder, like a fish in a little puddle. Seeing them at odds with each other, fear came upon me.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The world around was volatile, all directions were in turmoil. Wanting a home for myself, I saw nowhere unsettled.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Yet even in their settlement they were at odds— seeing that, I grew uneasy. Then I saw a dart there, so hard to see, stuck in the heart.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When struck by that dart, you run around in all directions. But when that same dart has been plucked out, you neither run around nor sink down.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: (On that topic, the trainings are recited.) Whatever attachments there are in the world, don't pursue them. Having pierced through sensual pleasures in every way, train yourself for extinguishment.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Be truthful, not rude, free of deceit, and rid of slander; without anger, a sage would cross over the evils of greed and avarice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Prevail over sleepiness, sloth, and drowsiness, don't abide in negligence, A person intent on quenching would not stand for arrogance.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Don't be led into lying, or get caught up in affection for form. Completely understand conceit, and desist from hasty conduct.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Don't relish the old, or welcome the new. Don't grieve for what is running out, or get attached to things that pull you in.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Greed, I say, is the great flood, and longing is the current— the basis, the compulsion, the swamp of sensuality so hard to get past.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: The sage never strays from the truth; the brahmin stands on solid ground. Having given up everything, they are said to be at peace.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They have truly known, they're a knowledge master, understanding the teaching, they are independent. They rightly proceed in the world, not coveting anything here.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One who has crossed over sensuality here, the chain in the world so hard to get past, grieves not, nor hopes; they've cut the strings, they're no longer bound.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: What came before, let wither away, and after, let there be nothing. If you don't grasp at the middle, you will live at peace.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One who has no sense of ownership in the whole realm of name and form, does not grieve for that which is not, they suffer no loss in the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If you don't think of anything as belonging to yourself or others, not finding any possessiveness, you won't grieve, thinking "I don't have it".

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not bitter, not fawning, unstirred, everywhere even; when asked about one who is unwavering, I declare that that is the benefit.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For the unstirred who understand, there's no performance of deeds. Desisting from instigation, they see sanctuary everywhere.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A sage doesn't speak of themselves as being among superiors, inferiors, or equals. Peaceful, rid of stinginess, they are neither ditching nor taking up.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Never before have I seen," said Venerable Sāriputta, "or heard from anyone about a teacher of such graceful speech, come from Tusita heaven to lead a community.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: To all the world with its gods he appears as a Clear-eyed One who has dispelled all darkness, and alone attained to bliss.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: On behalf of the many here still bound, I have come seeking with a question to that Buddha, unattached and impartial, free of deceit, come to lead a community.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Suppose a mendicant who loathes attachment frequents a lonely lodging— the root of a tree, a charnel ground, on mountains, or in caves.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: In these many different lodgings, how many dangers are there at which a mendicant in their silent lodging ought not tremble?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: On their journey to the untrodden place, how many adversities are there in the world that must they overcome in their remote lodging?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: What ways of speech should they have? Of what kind is their alms resort? What precepts and vows should a resolute mendicant uphold?

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having undertaken what training, unified, alert, and mindful, would they purge their own stains, like a smith smelting silver?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "If one who loathes attachment frequents a lonely lodging," said the Buddha to Sāriputta, "in their search for awakening—as accords with the teaching— I shall tell you, as I understand it, what is comfortable for them.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: An attentive one, a mindful mendicant living on the periphery should not be afraid of five perils: flies, mosquitoes, reptiles, human contact, or four-legged creatures.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Nor should they fear followers of other teachings, even having seen the many threats they pose. And then one seeking the good should overcome any other adversities.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Afflicted by illness and hunger, they should endure cold and excessive heat. Though afflicted by many such things, the homeless one should exert energy, firmly striving.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They must not steal or lie; and should touch creatures firm or frail with love. If they notice any clouding of the mind, they should dispel it as Māra's ally.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: They must not fall under the sway of anger or arrogance; having dug them out by the root, they would stand firm. Then, faced with likes and dislikes, they would surely overcome.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Putting wisdom in the foremost place, rejoicing in goodness, they would put an end to those adversities. They'd vanquish discontent in their remote lodging. And they'd vanquish the four lamentations:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: 'What will I eat? Where will I eat? Oh, I slept badly! Where will I sleep?' The trainee, the migrant without abode, would dispel these lamentable thoughts.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Receiving food and clothes in due season, they would know moderation for the sake of contentment. Guarded in these things, walking restrained in the village, they wouldn't speak harshly even when provoked.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Eyes downcast, not footloose, devoted to absorption, they'd be very wakeful. Grounded in equanimity, serene, they should cut off worrisome habits of thought.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: A mindful one would welcome reproach, and would dissolve hard-heartedness toward their spiritual companions. They may utter skillful speech, but not for too long, and they shouldn't provoke people to blame.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: And there are five more taints in the world, for the removal of which the mindful one should train, vanquishing desire for sights, sounds, flavors, smells, and touches.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having removed desire for these things, a mindful mendicant, their heart well freed, rightly investigating the Dhamma in good time, at one, would banish the darkness."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: From the fair city of the Kosalans to the southern region came a brahmin expert in hymns, aspiring to nothingness.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He settled in a region under the shared dominion of Assaka and Muḷaka, where he lived on the bank of the Godāvarī River, getting by on gleanings and fruit.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: He was supported by a prosperous village nearby. With the revenue earned from there he performed a great sacrifice.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When he had completed the great sacrifice, he returned to his hermitage once more. Upon his return, another brahmin arrived.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Foot-sore and thirsty, with grotty teeth and dusty head, he approached the other and asked for five hundred coins.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When Bāvari saw him, he invited him to sit down, asked of his happiness and well-being, and said the following.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Whatever I had available to give, I have already distributed. Believe me, brahmin, I don't have five hundred coins."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "If, good fellow, you do not give me what I ask, then on the seventh day, let your head explode in seven!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: After performing a ritual, that charlatan uttered his dreadful curse. When he heard these words, Bāvari became distressed.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Not eating, he grew emaciated, stricken by the dart of sorrow. And in such a state of mind, he could not enjoy absorption.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Seeing him anxious and distraught, a goddess wishing to help, approached Bāvari and said the following.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "That charlatan understands nothing about the head, he only wants money. When it comes to heads or head-splitting, he has no knowledge at all."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Then you, Madam, must know— please answer my question. Let me hear what you say about heads and head-splitting."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I too do not know that, I have no knowledge in that matter. When it comes to heads or head-splitting, it is the Victors who have vision."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "So who then, in all this vast territory, does know about heads and head-splitting? Please tell me, goddess."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "From the city of Kapilavatthu the World Leader has gone forth. He is a scion of King Okkāka, a Sakyan, and a beacon.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: For he, brahmin, is the Awakened One! He has gone beyond all things; he has attained to all knowledge and power; his eye sees clearly in all things, he has attained the end of all deeds; he is freed with the ending of attachments.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That Buddha, the Blessed One in the world, the Clear-eyed One, teaches Dhamma. Go to him and ask— he will answer you."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When he heard the word "Buddha", Bāvari was elated. His sorrow faded, and he was filled to brimming with joy.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Uplifted, elated, and inspired, Bāvari questioned that goddess: "But in what village or town, or in what land is the protector of the world, where we may go and pay respects to the Awakened One, best of men?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Near Sāvatthī, home of the Kosalans, is the Victor abounding in wisdom, vast in intelligence. That Sakyan is indefatigable, free of defilements, that captain of men understands head-splitting."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Therefore he addressed his acolytes, brahmins who had mastered the hymns: "Come, students, I shall speak. Listen to what I say.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Today has arisen in the world one whose appearance in the world is hard to find again— he is renowned as the Awakened One. Quickly go to Sāvatthī and see the best of men."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Brahmin, how then are we to know the Buddha when we see him? We don't know, please tell us, so we can recognize him."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The marks of a great man have been handed down in our hymns. Thirty-two have been described, complete and in order.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: One upon whose body is found these marks of a great man has two possible destinies, there is no third.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If he stays at home, having conquered this land without rod or sword, he shall govern by principle.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: But if he goes forth from the lay life to homelessness, he becomes an Awakened One, a perfected one, with veil cast off, supreme.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Ask him about my birth, clan, and marks, my hymns and acolytes; and further, about heads and head-splitting— but do so only in your mind!

author: Gotama Buddha
text: If he is the Buddha of unhindered vision, he will answer with his voice the questions in your mind."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Sixteen brahmin acolytes heard what Bāvari said: Ajita, Tissametteyya, Puṇṇaka and Mettagū,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Dhotaka and Upasīva, Nanda and then Hemaka, both Todeyya and Kappa, and Jatukaṇṇī the astute,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Bhadrāvudha and Udaya, and the brahmin Posāla, Mogharāja the intelligent, and Piṅgiya the great seer.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Each of them had their own following, they were renowned the whole world over. Those attentive ones, meditators who love absorption, were redolent with the potential of their past deeds.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Having bowed to Bāvari, and circled him to his right, they set out for the north, with their dreadlocks and hides.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: First to Patiṭṭhāna of Muḷaka, then on to the citadel of Māhissatī; to Ujjenī and Gonaddhā, and Vedisa, and Vanasa.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then to Kosambī and Sāketa, and the capital city of Sāvatthī; on they went to Setavyā and Kapilavatthu, and the homestead at Kusinārā.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: To Pāvā they went, and Bhoga City, and on to Vesālī and the Magadhan city. Finally they reached the Pāsāṇaka Shrine, fair and delightful.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Like a thirsty person to cool water, like a merchant to great profit, like a heat-struck person to shade, they quickly climbed the mountain.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: At that time the Buddha, at the fore of the mendicant Saṅgha, was teaching the mendicants the Dhamma, like a lion roaring in the jungle.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Ajita saw the Buddha, like the sun shining with a hundred rays, like the moon on the fifteenth day when it has come into its fullness.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Then he saw his body, complete in all features. Thrilled, he stood to one side and asked this question in his mind.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Speak about the brahmin's birth; of his clan; and his own marks; what hymns is he proficient in; and how many he teaches."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "His age is a hundred and twenty. By clan he is a Bāvari. There are three marks on his body. He is a master of the three Vedas,

author: Gotama Buddha
text: the teachings on the marks, the testaments, the vocabularies, and the rituals. He teaches recitation to five hundred, and has reached proficiency in his own teaching."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "O supreme man, cutter of craving, please reveal in detail Bāvari's marks— let us doubt no longer!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "He can cover his face with his tongue; there is a tuft of hair between his eyebrows; his private parts are sheathed in a foreskin: know them as this, student."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Hearing the answers without having heard any questions, all the people, inspired, with cupped palms, wondered:

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Who is it that asked a question with their mind? Was it a god or divinity? Or Indra, Sujā's husband? To whom does the Buddha reply?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Bāvari asks about heads and head-splitting. May the Buddha please answer, and so, O seer, dispel our doubt."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Know ignorance as the head, and knowledge as the head-splitter, when joined with faith, mindfulness, and immersion, and enthusiasm and energy."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: At that, the student, full of inspiration, arranged his antelope-skin cloak over one shoulder, and fell with his head to the Buddha's feet.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Good fellow, the brahmin Bāvari together with his acolytes, elated and happy, bows to your feet, O Clear-eyed One!"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "May the brahmin Bāvari be happy, together with his acolytes. And may you, too, be happy! May you live long, student.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: To Bāvari and you all I grant the opportunity to clear up all doubt. Please ask whatever you want."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: Granted the opportunity by the Buddha, they sat down with cupped palms. Ajita asked the Realized One the first question right there. The introductory verses are finished.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "By what is the world shrouded?" said Venerable Ajita. "Why does it not shine? Tell me, what is its sullying? What is its greatest fear?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The world is shrouded in ignorance." replied the Buddha. "Avarice and negligence make it not shine. Muttered prayer is its sullying, I say. Suffering is its greatest fear."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The streams flow everywhere," said Venerable Ajita. "What is there to block them? And tell me the restraint of streams— by what are they locked out?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "The streams in the world," replied the Buddha, "are blocked by mindfulness. I tell you the restraint of streams— they are locked out by wisdom."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "That wisdom and mindfulness," said Venerable Ajita, "and that which is name and form, good fellow; when questioned, please tell me of this: where does this all cease?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "This question which you have asked, I shall answer you, Ajita. Where name and form cease with no residue left behind— with the cessation of consciousness, here they cease."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "There are those who have appraised the teaching, and many kinds of trainees here. Now you, being alert, are asked to tell me their behavior, good fellow."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Not greedy for sensual pleasures, their mind would be unclouded. Skilled in all things, a mendicant would wander mindful."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Who here in the world is content?" said Venerable Tissametteyya. "Who has no perturbations? What thoughtful one, knowing both ends, is not stuck in the middle? Who do they say is a great man? Who here has escaped the seamstress?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Leading the spiritual life among sensual pleasures," replied the Buddha, "rid of craving, ever mindful; a mendicant who, after appraisal, is quenched: that's who has no perturbations.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: That thoughtful one, knowing both ends, is not stuck in the middle. He is a great man, I declare; he has escaped the seamstress here."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "To the imperturbable, the seer of the root," said Venerable Puṇṇaka, "I have come seeking with a question. On what grounds have seers and men, aristocrats and brahmins here in the world performed so many different sacrifices to the gods? I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Whatever seers and men," replied the Buddha, "aristocrats and brahmins here in the world have performed so many different sacrifices to the gods: all performed sacrifices bound to old age, longing for this place."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "As to those seers and men," said Venerable Puṇṇaka, "and aristocrats and brahmins here in the world who have performed so many different sacrifices to the gods: being diligent in the technique of sacrifice, have they crossed over rebirth and old age, good fellow? I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Hoping, invoking, praying, and worshiping," replied the Buddha, "they pray for pleasure derived from profit. Devoted to sacrifice, besotted by rebirth, they've not crossed over rebirth and old age, I declare."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "If those devoted to sacrifice," said Venerable Puṇṇaka, "have not, by sacrificing, crossed over rebirth and old age, who then in the world of gods and humans has crossed over rebirth and old age, good fellow? I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "Having appraised the world high and low," replied the Buddha, "there is nothing in the world that disturbs them. Peaceful, unclouded, untroubled, with no need for hope— they've crossed over rebirth and old age, I declare."

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this," said Venerable Mettagū, "for I think you are a knowledge master, evolved. Where do all these sufferings come from, in all their countless forms in the world?"

author: Gotama Buddha
text: "You have rightly asked me of the origin of suffering," replied the Buddha, "I shall tell you as I understand it. Attachment is the source of suffering in all its countless forms in the world.

author: Gotama Buddha
text: When an ignorant person builds up attachments, that dullard returns to suffering again and again. So let one who understands not build up attachments, contemplating the inception of suffering and rebirth."
